Alia deinde ex eadem posteriore trunci sede, sed sub secundum, V. da prodit, quae descendens, & ligamentum transuersum transiens, per pedis dorsum excurrit, in digitos abducentes musculos diffusa. Reliquum trunci per tibiae posteriora, deorsum fertur, & circa malleolum internum pedi furculum offert, qui pollicum adit, & pedis dorsum perreptat. Ipse autem truncus inter tendines musculorum digitorum pedis latens, in duos ramos diffecatur, quorum interior pollici duos, duos indici, vnum medio: exterior vero duos minimo, duos huic proximis digitis, inferiore fedelargitur. Ceterum, etsi arteriarum progressus magna ex parte talis fit, qualem descripsimus, quod tamen supra de Venis diximus, non solum pro indiuiduorum diuersitate, sed etiam laterum in eodem homine, ipsorum distributionem plurimum variare, id etiam de arteriis tenendum est, quae aliis hominibus alio modo se habent.

# CAPVT VI.

*Vena arterialis, & Arteriae venalis historiam complectitur.*

<margin>Vena arterialis. Arteria venalis.</margin>
<margin>Ortus.</margin>

<margin>Distribuitio.</margin>

VT perfecta omnibusque suis numeris absoluta sit haec de Venis & Arteriis tractatio, colophonis loco historiam tertiae Venae & secundae arteriae nobis apponere libuit. Vocatur Vena, arterialis, & Vena quidem ab officio, quod Veteres sanguinem deferre ex dextro cordis ventriculo credidissent: at arterialis a tunica, arteriarum membranae simili, cum simplex non sit, vt Venarum, sed gemina. Arteria contra, venalis dicitur, & arteria quidem, quod aerem deuehere, attractum per pulmones Antiqui statuerint: Venalis autem, quod substantia corpori venarum respondeat, cum simplex sit tunica, nec admodum crassa. Reiecimus autem vtriusque tractationem in hunc praecipue locum, vt vtraque simul ageremus, cum & ex eodem viscere nascantur, & in idem inferantur, praeterea que eadem distributione gaudeant. Enascuntur enim ex Corde, & Vena quidem ex editiore sede dextri ventriculi: Arteria autem ex sinistri. Implantatur autem & exhauritur vtraque; in Pulmonum substantiam, & Vena quidem per dextrum asperae arteriae latus porrigitur, Arteria autem per sinistrum. Mox in duos vtraque secatur ramos, quorum alter ad dextram, alter ad sinistram pulmonum partem abit, vtroque iterum bifariam secto, atque his in ramos alios, donec in minutissimos furculos dispergantur. Rami autem maiores sese inuicem comitantur, vt vena cum arteria perpetuo incedat, multis anastomobibus iunctae, in quarum medio asperae arteriae rami excurrunt. Insignia autem vasa sunt, maioraque longe, quam pulmonum magnitudo requirere videtur, cum partes illae, vt diximus libro superiore, quae plurimum dissipant alimenti, venas ampliores requirunt, nulla autem fit, quae pulmonibus ob perpetuum

<meta>continues from previous page: ...The trunk of the great artery, when it arrives at the last vertebra of the loins, along with the entire duct we have described, follows a path below the vena cava to the left, so that it might ascend the vein, lest it be worn away by the hardness of the sacral bone during that continuous movement. It is divided, however, not unlike the Cava itself, into two notable branches, which those skilled in anatomy call the Iliac arteries because of their position, and carried obliquely downward to the thigh, they express the inverted Y of the Greeks. These themselves also, before they are brought into the thigh, provide many branches, just like the iliac veins, to which they respond exactly in every way.</meta>

<margin>Sacral.</margin>
From the lower seat of the artery, before the Iliacs are divided, the <term>Sacral</term> [arteries] emerge, which are notable and, carried downward resting upon the sacral bone, they enter its foramina, and run out to its marrow and the posterior parts of the sacral bone. And through these, too, is a path for the matter causing colicky pain, so that it may effect paralysis of the legs. Hence, a little below the division of the trunk, the Iliacs are subdivided into two branches, of which one is inner and smaller: the other outer and larger.

<margin>Propagations of the Iliac arteries. Of the inner, or smaller. 1. Muscular. 2. Hypogastric.</margin>
The smaller, or inner Iliac, leads out two propagations, one from the outer, the other from the inner seat. The <term>Outer</term>, commonly called the Muscular, [is called] by us by the stricter name, <term>Gluteal</term>, because it descends with the vein of the same name between the sacrum and the hip bone, where they depart from each other, and it extends several shoots into the muscles overlying the ilium bone, called the Gluteals because they are the authors of the buttocks. The <term>Inner</term> is called the <term>Hypogastric</term>, which is quite notable and ample, and carried straight downward to the lower seat of the sacral bone, it bestows certain shoots in men upon the fundus and neck of the bladder, and then also upon the rectum, which can also be called the hemorrhoidal arteries. In women, however, for whom this branch is slightly larger, besides the said parts, it distributes a numerous propagation also into the lower region of the fundus of the uterus, and likewise into its neck. Hence, one may seek the reason why, if the uterus proceeds to the middle of the hip, convulsions occur, as Hippocrates testifies in his book, *On the Nature of Women*. Likewise, if the uterus has settled toward the hip, why menses are suppressed, and pain occurs in the lower belly and in the softness of the sides. For the blood, which is driven by Nature to the uterus, when the arteries are compressed by the settling, cannot be deposited in the uterus, whence necessarily regurgitating, it fills the neighboring veins and arteries, which, swelling, cause these pains. We have often seen in dissections that these veins were so turgid that they were seven times larger than themselves. From this also, the reason can be given for that aphorism, which is the thirty-second of the fifth section, in the same Hippocrates, where he testifies that in a woman vomiting blood, relief occurs upon the eruption of the menses. Which, indeed, happens by the consent of all through revulsion, and truly cannot occur through the benefit of the veins, because the veins of the stomach arise from the portal vein, but those of the uterus from the cava; no other consensus is to be sought than that which occurs through the arteries, especially since the hypogastric artery is not far distant from the coeliac. From these, similarly, the reason will be rendered for the aphorism following this one, where, when menses are deficient, he deems a nosebleed to be salutary.

<margin>Umbilical artery.</margin>
The remaining part of the smaller Iliac descends and brings out the <term>Umbilical artery</term>, which is carried along the length of the great artery and is connected by strong membranes to the sides of the urinary bladder. It loses its cavity in those who have emerged into these pleasant breaths of life, which, how it is done, we shall show later in the ninth book at greater length.

<summary>This page describes the division of the Iliac arteries into the sacral, gluteal, hypogastric, and umbilical branches, detailing their anatomical paths and functions in the lower torso.</summary>

In Mulieribus vero, quibus paulo amplior hic ramus est, præter dictas partes, etiam in inferiorem vteri fundi regionem, & pariter in illius ceruicem numerosam propaginem distribuit. Hinc rationem licet petere, ob quam si Vteri ad medium coxendicis processerint, conuulsiones fiant, vt testatur Hippocrates, lib. de natura muliebri. Item, si Vterus ad coxam decubuerit, cur menses supprimantur, & dolor fiat in imo ventre, & in laterum mollitudine. Sanguis enim, qui ad Vterum à Natura pellitur, arteriis compressis à decubitu, in vterum deponi non potest, vnde necessario regurgitans, vicinas Venas & Arterias replet, quæ intumescentes dolores hos efficiunt. Vidimus enim sæpenumero in dissectionibus sic turgidas fuisse has venas, vt septuplo sese ampliores fuerint. Hinc etiam ratio reddi potest aphorismi illius, qui est trigesimus secundus quintæ sectionis, apud eundem Hippocratem, vbi Mulieri sanguinem vomenti erumpentibus mensibus solutionem fieri testatur. Quod sane, cum omnium consensu fiat per reuulsionem, & vero Venarum beneficio contingere nequeat, quod Venæ Ventriculi à Portæ vena, at Vteri, à Caua oriantur, non alius consensus quærendus est, quam ille, qui fit per Arterias, maxime cum nec arteria hypogastrica procul à Cœliaca distet. Ex his similiter ratio reddetur sequentis hunc aphorismi, vbi mensibus deficientibus hæmorrhagiam narium salutarem censet. 

<margin>Arteria Vmbilicalis.</margin>
Reliqua pars Iliacæ minoris descendit, & t arteriam Vmbilicalem educit, t, η.η. quæ iuxta longitudinem arteriæ magnæ defertur, validisque membranis Vesicæ vrinariæ lateribus connectitur. Cauitatem autem amittit in iis, qui in has iucundas vitæ auras prodiere, quod quomodo fiat, postmodum libro nono pluribus ostensuri sumus.

Harum usum omnes fere, qui hactenus in Anatomicis aliquid scripserunt, unanimi consensu prodiderunt esse, vt Vena quidem pulmonibus alimentum afferat, Arteria autem à pulmonibus haustum aerem ad Cor deducat. Quae opinio absurdissimo fundamento nititur, sanguinem scilicet nulla ratione in hac arteria contineri, in quo confutando prolixiores ellemus, nisi anatomicam inspectionem, & experientiam satis superque falsitatem demonstrare sciremus. Quare ab iis potius standum existimo, qui à dextro cordis ventriculo ad pulmones per Venam arterialem sanguinem transmitti credunt, & hinc in Arteriam venalem per anastomoses deduci, à qua postea ad Cor transportatur, vbi magis elaboratur sanguis ille dextri ventriculi, & fit spirituosus, sicque per Arteriam magnam in vniuersum corpus, pro vita singularum partium, pellitur. Nec verum est aerem in Arteriam venalem rapi, cum foramina ibi nulla sint, sed aer qui per Laryngem in asperam pulmonum arteriam raptus est, bronchia omnia refrigerat, quod frigus cum adiacentibus vasis communicetur (diximus enim vbique bronchia ferri in medio Venae arteriosae & Arteriae venosae) refrigerat simul sanguinem in ipsis contentum, qui Cor ingrediens calorem illum nimium attemperat, vt propterea opus non sit aerem in substantia ad Cor transferri.

Temperare mihi non possum, quo minus de quaestione vexatissima nonnulla suggeram: an et Tragoediae Senecam Philosophum Autorem agnoscant? Notum enim est, quomodo communiter tres Senecae nomine insignes recenseantur: M. Annaeus Rhetor, L. Annaeus Seneca Philosophus, et tandem Seneca Tragoedus. Legi de hoc possunt Bailleti jugemens des Sçauans sur les principaux ouvrages des Auteurs Tomo IV. Parte II. pagina 363. et Autores sub finem citati. Sane diversa eruditi de Tragoediis sentiunt. Non unius esse autoris, modo dicta judicia afferunt; asserit etiam Clarissimus Fabricius loco citato dum Herculem furentem M. Annaeo Senecae, Patri, Hippolytum Senecae Philosopho, et ita reliquas, alias aliis Autoribus vindicat. Those who concern themselves with the philosopher <term>Lucius Annaeus Seneca</term> customarily weigh his name, lineage, credibility, writings, the sharpness of his style, and his dogmas in the balance, and examine each part diligently. Indeed, from the fact that he is called Lucius Annaeus Seneca, some authors—and among them Stadius—confuse Lucius Annaeus Seneca with the historian <term>Lucius Annaeus Florus</term>; this is quite absurd and was rightly noted by Salmasius in his notes and corrections to Florus. For the monuments of history and the verses in which Florus and the Emperor Hadrian vied with each other—"I do not wish to be Caesar, and so forth," "I do not wish to be Florus, and so forth"—abundantly prove how Florus was a contemporary of Trajan and Hadrian. Consult the most elegant program LXIV of the most illustrious Marcus Rosenb. on Florus. Conversely, Lucius Annaeus Seneca lived in the time of Nero, in the first century after the birth of Christ, as Suetonius in *Nero*, chapter 35, Dio Cassius, and others teach. Even if Vossius, a great ornament to the world of letters, concedes that Florus originated from the family of Seneca because his poetic diction savors of a poetic house, I add: the name Annaeus, which is the family name and belongs to Florus as well, testifies that he traced his origin to the same Annaean family. 

To approach more closely the noble lineage of Seneca: there was Marcus Annaeus Seneca the Rhetor, a most learned man of the Equestrian order, who in Corduba in Baetican Spain took to wife Elvia, also a Spaniard and a woman of great talent, and had three sons: Lucius Annaeus Seneca the philosopher, just mentioned; Annaeus Novatus; and Annaeus Mella, the father of Annaeus Lucanus, the author of the *Pharsalia*, that is, the history of the civil war between Caesar and Pompey, which ended on the Pharsalian plains. Lipsius gave us this pedigree of the Annaean family in *Electiones*, Book I, chapter 1, page 463 of his *Opera Critica*, as well as in the preface prefixed to the 1649 Leiden edition of the works of Seneca. Indeed, for one who has at hand those who have recorded the life of Seneca—among whom we count Jannutius Mannettus of Florence and Lipsius himself, who wrote a singular book on the life of Seneca—there is no reason to doubt that one might have accurate information regarding the condition of his life, his death, and other matters. 

The illustrious Lord von Ziegler presented the life of Seneca to the learned world in the vernacular tongue, using Tacitus, Suetonius, Dio, and others, in the *täglichen Schau-Platz der Zeit* [Daily Theater of the Times], April 30, pages 482, 483, 484. Regarding the Christian faith of Seneca, and whether he professed the same, not only did Lord Strauch, a professor at Wittenberg, deal with it in a peculiar dissertation in 1668, but also the blessed Kortholt—first at Rostock, later a truly Christian Professor of Theology at the illustrious <term>CHRISTIAN-ALBRECHT-UNIVERSITY</term> <gloss>Kiel</gloss> (as Lord Lindemann names him in the memorial of Christian Kortholt)—wished to address it in 1667 in his dissertation on the Christianity of Philip the Arab, Alexander Mammaea, Pliny the Younger, and Annaeus Seneca. "A law-expert and near-Christian Heathen," he is called by Lord Doctor Pfeiffer in *Anti-Mel*, Book I, page 19; add the epitaph to be found in Lord Ziegler at the cited location: "A Christian regarding the heathens," etc. These things are not in the least proven by the mutual letters of Paul and Seneca; they are ridiculous, inept, barbaric, and unworthy of Seneca and Paul, the fabrication of a rather unlearned monk. These are the words of Horn in his *History of Philosophy*, Book IV, where he discusses at greater length the religion of Seneca, by which he is said to have been a Christian, and refutes the arguments. One and the same craftsman composed the letters of Paul and Seneca, according to the judgment of the most Reverend Lord colleague, Lucius Ittig.

There is, moreover, a certain village called Neumbergk, far distant from Meissen. Yet it happened divinely that at one and the same time, Blessed Benno both performed a sacred rite there and was seen to be participating in sacred rites at Meissen. A certain Margrave of Meissen, being too greedy for property, when he had rushed into possession of the goods of the Meissen church through the greatest wickedness, Blessed Benno affirmed that the man would do well if he restored those things which he had snatched from the Meissen church itself, but if not, that God would some day seek penalties from him for such great impropriety. At which words the raging man was stirred and struck the most holy man with a slap. Then Blessed Benno, inspired by a divine spirit, said: "God Almighty will avenge this great injury at this same time of the following year." That insolent and proud Margrave mocked him, and a little later Blessed Benno began to be ill and, hoping that it would be brief so that he might migrate from this life to those above, whose companionship is sweet and eternal; a little before he died, he exhorted his canons to studiously embrace that charity which Christ taught us. Then he received the Eucharist, that divine food, with great piety, and when he had offered prayers to God, the best and greatest, he departed from life. And this, indeed, in the fortieth year of his pontificate, after Christ was born, one thousand one hundred and sixteen. Thus far concerning those things which, in his life, the divine man accomplished not by human counsel but divinely. We have decided to recite some of the things which happened with the greatest admiration after his death. And first, the Margrave, of whom we spoke a little before, when that time had arrived at which the holy man had predicted that the Margrave himself would pay the penalty, broke out into this voice: "Benno threatened in times past that some danger would happen to us on this day; he is dead; therefore, there is no reason for us to fear." Certainly, Christ is a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek, leaving no Vicar successor, other than His own holy Spirit, who will be present with His own always. Wherefore in the Melchizedekian priesthood of the New Testament (as was done once in the Old Aaronic one until the Messiah) we know of no pontifical succession. But we also know the succession of the Roman pontiffs, through various schisms and frequent antipopes, to have been foully interrupted in many ways and brutally contaminated: raging against one another with the most invidious and at the same time most atrocious censures. By what spirit they are led, their deeds prove, histories testify, poets sing, libraries speak, and the pious and learned lament. Bernard to Eugenius: What shall I say of the people? he says. They are the Roman people, and I could not open more briefly or more expressively what I feel about your parishioners. What is so well known to the age as the impudence and pride of the Romans? A people unaccustomed to peace, accustomed to tumult: a people harsh and intractable, up to now knowing not how to submit, unless it is unable to resist. The same Bernard: Woe, he says, to this generation from the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy, if it should even be called hypocrisy, which now cannot hide due to its abundance, and does not seek to due to its impudence. ->§. X.<-

Nor do we, even on account of the alleged reasons, posit anything dissenting from equity and honesty; rather, sound reason dictates duties toward God and neighbor, and what is that other than Piety? And although Religion, in so far as it promotes the salvation of souls, is to be drawn from peculiar divine revelation, yet it serves—as reason dictates—most especially for the promotion of the tranquility and sociality of this life, as <term>Pufendorf</term> <gloss>Samuel von Pufendorf, jurist</gloss> teaches in his *On the Duty of Man and Citizen*, book 1, chapter 3, §. 13. This utility, if it must be declared at greater length, redounds to both the Prince and the subjects; that he should show himself clement or good toward his subjects, and be uniquely intent upon the highest political good and the happiness of the Republic, that certainly is done by intuition of piety, the account of which is applied to him, since otherwise, that being neglected, he would take care of himself, not the people, would make no conscience of it, would oppress the citizens, would deprive them of their faculties, would expose justice itself for sale, or, to condense the matter, would give himself up to tyranny and decline into atheism, expecting the rebellion of subjects and his own resulting destruction, according to that:

> *Few kings descend to the son-in-law of Ceres without slaughter and blood, and few tyrants without a dry death.*

Likewise, the subjects, because they obey the supreme Ruler or Prince and comply with him in all things, they do so by intuition of piety: out of respect for which, even among spouses, among parents and children, and finally among Lords and servants, firm friendship and custom flourishes, whereas otherwise, without the existence of piety or religion, a war of all against

They think, however, that some provide nutritious juice to the nerves, others receive their waste, and reduce it through the lymphatic vessels into the veins, and others export their excrement outward, whence *Glisson* calls the first *nutritive*, the second *reductive*, and the third *excretory*. Those which are said to secrete the nutritious juice are the *mesenteric glands* and the *lumbar glands of Bartholin*: these glands are said to secrete *nutritious juice* from the chyle passing through the mesentery, which is then assumed by the nerves and carried to the brain: they call those *excretory* which emit their liquid outside the body or deposit it into a cavity, such as the *breasts, testicles*, and other glands: they call those *reductive* which take up the superfluous alible juice and reduce it again toward the veins; to which they refer, albeit incorrectly, the *parotids* and *jugulars*.

§. 55. But we do not approve this opinion either, for it rests upon that false hypothesis that the nerves carry nutritious juice, of which matter we must treat in a special exercise *on nutritive glands*; for I do not deny that some secrete nutritious juice, but I deny likewise that the mesaraic glands do so, as I argue where I deal with the *mesaraic glands*. Reductive glands are nothing other than excretory, for, as they themselves admit, they secrete lymph; that some lymph, however, is reduced into the blood mass, due to various uses, that does not properly pertain to the glands, whose unique and principal duty is to secrete something, whatever use that secreted liquid may be put to.

§. XIV. It is also not to be approved that boys and girls should be trained for this art of walking on a rope. Indeed, it is the duty of parents to take care that their children are instructed in arts that are useful for social and civil life. Our most blessed Lord Boeclerus excellently says in *Political Institutions*, book 3, page 45: "He warns parents to undertake the care of education seriously and constantly, sparing no labor, no expense, if indeed they love and revere the honest succession of their family, the utility of the State and the Fatherland—to which we must present not only ourselves but our own—and above all the authority of God, stimulated by the instincts implanted by nature and the holy laws toward the duties of parents." Parents have no regard for this duty of theirs who even teach their children the rope-dancing art themselves, and allow them to be instructed in it. Such are rightly said to sacrifice their dearest pledges to <term>Moloch</term> <gloss>a Canaanite deity associated with child sacrifice</gloss>, as far as in them lies. Long ago, the Blessed Cyprian, 1st Epistle, 10, very heavily resented that there were those among Christians who did not blush to teach the theatrical art: "I think," he says, "it is appropriate neither to the Divine Majesty nor to evangelical discipline that the modesty and honor of the Church be defiled by such a base and infamous contagion"; how much more heavily we believe he would have taken it that parents themselves instruct their children in such arts, which are unworthy of Christian piety and gravity.

§. XV. Furthermore, since the rope-dancing art ought not to be approved by Christians, the question arises whether it can be tolerated in a Christian State? Certainly the Fathers of the Church—Tertullian, Clement of Alexandria, Cyprian, Arnobius, Lactantius, Isidore, Augustine, Chrysostom, Salvianus (with whom the most learned Rittershusius's annotation on page 190 should be joined)—judge that they should be expelled from their Christian Republic, if we consider those things which they gravely warned about concerning spectacles. A certain booklet, written in our Germanic or common (if one prefers) tongue, titled Johannes Reuchlin's *Ocular Mirror*, appeared in the light—alas—partly through the printing press. His Imperial Majesty, who is to be celebrated by the letters and tongues of all, not undeservedly prohibited it by his open letters throughout his entire empire—as it was dangerous to all and inclined more than was just toward the favor of Jewish perfidy—from being sold, bought, kept, or publicly disseminated, and he forbade it, led primarily by justice. Now this command of our most serene Emperor, being so holy and salutary, was executed with the utmost equity by the most reverend lords in Christ, the Archbishops of the dioceses of Mainz and Cologne, and also by the most sacred prelates of the churches of Worms and Würzburg. As a result, in Frankfurt, that most noble emporium of all Germany, and in the public fairs there, many of these dangerous booklets were intercepted and held by public decree and most holy law, lest they be disseminated more widely and cause greater scandal to the unrefined populace. ¶ Then, in the year 1513, around April, when the same author, inflated by I know not what spirit, had brought to light for the defense of his booklet another—but a most biting and (if I may say so) most injurious—pamphlet, the sacred Imperial Majesty, out of zeal for the faith, committed by public edict to the most sacred Archbishops of Mainz, Cologne, and Trier, as well as the Inquisitors of heretical depravity, the task of exterminating the scandals from the simple Christian faithful (as has been said above), insofar as they would strive with their strength for the worthy suppression of the recent booklets of the aforementioned Johannes Reuchlin and labor completely and entirely. This most equitable imperial mandate, when it had been offered to the Inquisitor—a man of the utmost integrity and goodness—wishing first of all not to fail in the causes of the orthodox faith due to his office, and to satisfy the imperial command (as was fitting), he offered the booklet or *Ocular Mirror* of said doctor before all else, and first in the process (so that he might not attempt anything rashly nor tremble afterward in any way), to be weighed by the universities of Louvain, Cologne, Erfurt, and thereafter Mainz—diverse but most famous universities—as being more suitable and closer to him, requesting only this for the common good of all: that through the counsel and final judgment of men most learned in divine law, he might not be ignorant of what was worthy to be done in this present business offered to him, and that he might bring forth fruit eternally salutary to the Church of God. ¶ After, therefore, by most diligent examination, with the collation of the principal booklet (which bears the name *Ocular Mirror*) to his other subsequent defenses

The *Preservative* is occupied with the prohibition of a new influx, and how the remaining morbific causes can be suffocated as if in the herb, by eliminating that which can harm by quantity, and altering that which can harm by quality.

The *Vital* regards the strength of both the whole and the affected parts, and commands one to preserve what remains of health through good nourishment, to correct the parts that send [the humor] through appropriate medicines, and to corroborate and fortify those that receive [it] through both suitable foods and medicines.

**The material of the remedy is to be sought from three customary sources.**

From the **SURGICAL** first is *Venesection* <gloss>bloodletting</gloss>. Since the source and cause of the evil lies in the blood mass, and this, being abundant in the body and vessels, is stirred up with vicious motion and as it were boils, and the pain attracts the matter more and more to the affected parts so that arthritis is increased or fever succeeds, it will not be ill-advised, provided the strength, age, and concomitant symptoms permit, to open the vein opposite the affected part in the beginning; naturally, if the pain persists in the right arm, [open] the vein of the left, and conversely; but if the foot or hip suffers, [open] the one placed directly, namely in the same side of the elbow or even the ham or the ankle, called the Sciatic, sometimes, according to *Plater*, to cut [it] in the healthy leg, and to extract a just, not excessive, quantity of blood, and always in this operation to look to a good configuration of the heavens.

I am furthermore excluded by the narrowness of time, which scarcely allows it to be granted to add a few things about his disease and its last act, his blessed, I say, passing. Concerning his illness, I think you should recognize the words of the Doctor of Medicine.

Regarding the illness, I would not incorrectly call it hepatic <note>affecting the liver</note>. For as the blessed Lord Rector had a constitution of the whole body that was too hot and dry, so also I observed his liver to be of the same temperament, a fertile mother of bilious humors. There was a close relationship of this to Scurvy. The humors burgeoning from such a constitution attacked the liver above all, the seat of its dominion, obstructing a good part of it. At the beginning, the patient felt a pain of a certain kind weighing down in this organ, and soon his appetite was prostrated, and at the same time his nightly rest failed. It was time to look around for remedies and to expel the snake hiding in the first grass. However, such was the ardor for study in the excellent Master, such was his care for his students, that he took greater account of them than of himself.

With the humors impacted in the liver, time and opportunity were left for it to strengthen its dominion; hence, little by little, everything began to turn for the worse. Nearly months, not weeks, had passed since his body, never accustomed to illness, had felt the first movements of the lurking enemy. The matter in the liver had already visibly turned into fermentation: the mass of the blood, at the same time, with the contamination of rot communicated, while the Blessed one allowed medicine to be made for himself. He committed the business of his care to his kinsman and physician, Lord Johann Köcker. He omitted nothing that he could do for the preservation of the Eximite Man, his most dear friend.

All those who truly profess to be lovers of political science, and who rightly apply their effort to examining and investigating the laws of nature, judge gravely that for the blessed life of citizens, it is required not only that the state be endowed with great glory, rich in resources, and firm in wealth, but also that it be honorable through virtue. For although those to whom, having abandoned virtue, nothing is lacking for the convenience of all things, seem to some to live well and securely enough, yet it is so far from the case that this, separated from the honesty of morals, should be called true happiness, that on the contrary, we do not hesitate to say it possesses an empty and most deceitful appearance of mutable things and insidious enticements. They have therefore erred vehemently, as many among the ancients as maintained that there is no natural law; that all laws should either be proposed, or changed, or rejected, according to the utility of each person; that it is fitting for every mortal, with nature showing the way, to consider only that which is useful; that justice is to be valued at nothing; and that it is the height of stupidity to propose rewards and honors for good deeds, and punishments and ignominy for evil deeds; for this, they claim, is to afflict oneself with damages while producing profit for others; and that even the most powerful peoples, masters of the whole world, must perish if they return all things to others and employ justice and equity in all their dealings.

# Master PETER HENDEL,

->Councilor of the Court of the Varisci, Scholarch of the Gymnasium, Advocate of Causes, et cetera.<-

->*His Patron, to be honored with observance*<-

->Offers his most abundant greetings.<-

### GEORG Steinhagen.

You see, I believe, what I am doing, most distinguished of men. I, a mere stranger, rise to the dignity of your status. See, however, how I justify to myself the logic of this duty. You, when I was hoping for no such thing and had earned nothing, willed that I, a stranger, should be among the number of your own; and should I not honor you, no longer a stranger, but known to me through the greatest benevolence? Seneca rightly says: That favor is pleasant and will live in the mind, which comes of its own accord. How dearly, then, must you think you are held in my mind, you who have laid claim to me of your own volition through the testimony of your highest regard? When I consider this, I see what I owe; when I think how I might conveniently repay it, I find no way. Unless you accept a good intention and deem him to have satisfied his debt who confesses that he owes it. Behold, therefore, these papers as a sponsor for this debt, and I ask that you accept them with an equitable mind. Truly, I would not offend the public good by calling you to read these trifles; but another, in turn, shall not command my mind, so that I might honor anyone other than You, with whom alone it is now permitted for me to confer honor.

### GEORGIUS Steinhagen.

Vides, credo, quid agam, Virorum Amplissime. peregrini soli civis dignitatis tuae fascibus assurgo. Vide verò quàm et officii hujus ratio mihi constet. Tu nihil me tale sperantem, nihil meritum, peregrinum, tuorum numero prior esse voluisti: ego verò te, non jam alienum, sed summâ benevolentiâ mihi cognitum non observem ? Sapienter Seneca; Illud beneficium jucundum, victurumque in animo est, quod obviam venit. Quàm tu ergò eximiè charum animo te meo esse putes, qui summi studii testificatione ultro me occupasti ? Hoc cum reputo, quid debeam, video: cum, quo pacto commodus exsolvam, cogito, non invenio. Nisi bonam mentem accipis, et satisfecisse illum existimas, qui debere se fatetur. Ejus verò sponsorem tenues ecce has chartas, quas aequo animo ut admittas, rogo. Equidem in publica commoda non peccem, ut te ad has legendas ineptias vocem ; sed alius vicissim animo meo non imperet, ut quemvis alium, quam Te, quo uno mihi nunc licet, honore prosequar.

### §. IX.

Furthermore, public scribes formerly obtained various names from the magistrates by whom they were either chosen or to whom they were attached, as Reinefius testifies in *Epist. XXXI to Rupert*, p. 168 (cf. Sigonius, loc. cit.). For Pontiffs, Dukes, Emperors, Consuls, Proconsuls, Aediles, Quaestors, and most other magistrates appointed their own specific scribes for themselves, who managed their business with writings and presided over the balancing of accounts, which were offered to the Republic when their magistracy was finished. Whence they were later called <term>Scribae Pontificum</term> <gloss>Scribes of the Pontiffs</gloss>, <term>Ducales</term>, <term>Imperatorii</term>, <term>Consulum</term>, <term>Proconsulum</term>, <term>Aedilium</term>, <term>Quaestorum</term>, and so forth; indeed, they were even called <term>Juris peritorum et Advocatorum</term> <gloss>Scribes of the Jurists and Advocates</gloss>. The ancients also used the term "leading of a funeral" in the same sense: Juvenal, *Satire* 1: *The funeral is led, to be applauded by angry friends.* On this matter, more shortly. The Romans were also called *Quirites* <gloss>Roman citizens</gloss> from *Quirinus* (Rosinus, Book II, Chapter XVII, *Roman Antiquities*; Gaius, Book I of the *Institutes*, Title 2, § 3), and likewise *Latini* <gloss>Latins</gloss> from *Latinus*, King of Italy, father-in-law of Aeneas (Rosinus, Book I, Chapter 1, *Roman Antiquities*).

## Thus was the Definition of the Name: the Definition of the Thing follows. Thesis V.

->*A funeral is the leading forth of the deceased, with customary rites, to a place designated for the honorable burial of bodies.*<-

Having completed those things which pertain to the definition of the name, we make an approach to the definition of the thing, since it explains the nature and essence of each thing (Bertius, Book IV, *Peripatetic Logic*, Chapter II). We place here, however, an essential definition, which consists of genus and difference (Horneius, Book IV, *Dialectics*, Chapter III, number 8). The genus is "leading forth," because leading belongs properly to funerals, as Servius holds on the *Georgics*, Book IV, although it also belongs to weddings; yet they have this word in common, as they have many common rites, such as the procession, torches, the bier, wreaths, ointments, and others, which Artemidorus also touched upon (Book II, Chapter LIV; Kirchmann, Book II, Chapter I, *On the Roman Funeral*). The other words of the definition contain the difference, which together constitute a causal definition: for the efficient cause of a funeral is the deceased, who also provide the material here; the formal cause are the customary rites, which are found in Rosinus (Book V, Chapter XXXIX, *Roman Antiquities*), Kirchmann, and others. The final cause is honorable burial, which is the highest happiness (Dempster on the cited passage of Rosinus), as also above in Thesis I, although there is another cause with respect to the living, namely, that bodies foul to sight and smell should be removed (Dempster, ibid.). Where one must simultaneously note the subject, the place designated for honorable burial, which for us is the cemetery (Gerhard, on the topic of death, § 90. See our Thesis XII).

## Thus conjunctively: it follows distinctly: then in the division of funerals. Thesis VI.

### And some funerals are indictive.

For although other distinctions arise from the different age, means, dignity, and last will of those to be buried: yet, with these being diligently considered, we find that funerals were of two kinds (Kirchmann, Book 1, Chapter IV, *On the Roman Funeral*), which distinction arose from games held in honor of the deceased, which they called funeral games, as witnessed by Rosinus (Book V, Chapter XXXIX, *Roman Antiquities*). The first kind is the Indictive Funeral: so called, according to Festus, because the people were called to it by a herald (Rosinus, loc. cit.). It is said to be from *indicendo* <gloss>proclaiming</gloss>, which word the ancients used in this meaning (Kirchmann, ibid.). Suetonius in *Caesar*: *The funeral being proclaimed, the pyre was built in the Field of Mars.* Cicero, in his *Oration for his House to the Pontiffs* and *On the Consular Provinces*. The illustrious Scaliger has observed the solemn words of this proclamation long ago from Terence (*Phormio*, Act V, last scene) and Varro (Book IV, *On the Latin Language*). Moreover, Indictive Funerals were most extensive, and besides other sumptuous equipment, were also celebrated with games (Cicero, Book II, *On the Laws*; Becmann, *On Origins*, p. 706; Rosinus and Kirchmann, in the cited places; Scaliger, Book I, *Ausonian Lectures*, Chapter XXVIII), with circus riders also employed (Festus Pompeius, Book XVII; Dempster on Rosinus, *Antiquities*, Book V, Chapter XXIV). The Public funeral can be referred to here, which was sometimes the same as the Indictive, as in Apuleius (Book 11, *Metamorphoses*), sometimes only a part of it, when, for instance, a cessation of business was proclaimed, or public mourning, or expenses were made from the public treasury (Kirchmann, ibid.). This honor was granted to Syphax, King of Numidia (Valerius Maximus, Book V, Chapter 1; Suetonius in *Vitellius*, Chapter III); to Sphaerus, Augustus’s freedman and tutor (Dio, Book XLVIII); to Piso, Urban Prefect (the same, Dio, Book LXIV). Illustrious women were not without a share of this (Idem, Book XLVII; Xiphilinus in *Tiberius*). There were furthermore various kinds of Public Funerals according to the diversity of honors managed by the deceased, such as Praetorian, Consular, Censorial, and Triumphal, as Polybius indicates (Book 6, *Histories*), where, however, Lipsius noted that the triumphal was confused with the censorial under the emperors. The most worthy was the Censorial, by which princes were carried out, such as Claudius (Tacitus, Book XII). Whence Spartianus in *Aelius Verus* calls it an Imperial funeral; in *Opilius Macrinus*, a Royal one. For the Censorship was the most honored among the magistracies (Plutarch in *Cato the Elder*).

Absolutis iis, quae ad nominis definitionem pertinent, accessum ad Rei definitionem facimus, quippè quae rei cujusque naturam, et essentiam explanat. *Bertius, Liber IV. Hic enim, cum Graecos Imperatores, à quibus Papa defecerant, novum sibi imperium moliti, timeret Romanae ultores perfidiae, et simul Aistulphum Longobardorum Regem ditioni Romanae, velut Graecorum imperio imminentem, demereri hoc novo perfidiae exemplo Pipinum placuit, in quo firmum adversus Graecos, et Longobardos praesidium haberet. Sub haec Bonifacio Moguntiae Antistiti, qui Romanos Sacrorum ritus, et dogmatum vanitatem primus in Germaniam melioribus jam alicubi imbutam intulit, munus à Zacharia demandatum est inungendi Pipini in Regem, quem ipsi Franci jam suis suffragiis delegissent. Legatis ergo in Franciam remeantibus unctio Pipini Suessione à Bonifacio peracta est, moxque Pipinus Rex dictus ab omnibus, et more gentis circumlatus clypeo, solioque impositus est. Ultimum deinde ad scenam claudendam actum confecit Childerici exauctoratio, qui ab rusticâ villâ, in qua degebat, ductus Ratisbonam in coenobium (uxorem Gisalam etiam destinabant Monasterio) scissâ caesarie, depositisque vestibus Monachum induit, nullâ graviore jacturâ, quàm crinium, cum regno, quod non obtinuerat, haud spoliaretur, et uxorem perdere forte in lucro sit. The rest of the nobles, the more prompt one was in service, the more he was elevated with wealth and honors, and having been increased by new things, they preferred the decorative and present to the old and vile. Nor did they distribute sacred and profane dignities to men of their own faction with less skill; they had distributed public offices to their friends as if it were their own right, and had cunningly transferred wealth consecrated to monasteries and churches to their clients, with the intention that everyone should desire only this: that the royal name and power should reside with him who would increase benefits, not overturn them.

<margin>Pippin prepares himself to occupy the kingdom.</margin>
Pippin, therefore, into whom alone the glory and authority of his father Martel and the administration of France had passed—after his brother Gripho was killed in the crossing of the Alps and the other, Carloman, had voluntarily embraced the monastic life—was driven by ambition to seize the kingdom. He saw himself flourishing in age, blessed with offspring, and supported by the love of all. The revenues of the kingdom, the dignities, fortresses, and soldiers were, like the nerves of a body or the gears of some automaton, turned and moved at his nod. He was, in the end, master of the kingdom in all but the name alone. Against him, Childeric was destitute not only of every aid but even of his own spirit, so unworthy of the royal title that he did not even pass for a man, and would have fallen headlong if pushed even by a finger.

For we see that in this battle some famous men, strenuous leaders, excellent centurions, and brave soldiers have been missed, because Mars picks off every strenuous man for himself and wagers on the bravest. We have received with the incredible grief of all that Augustinus Barbadicus, a man of the highest nobility, of excellent greatness of spirit, and of singular love for his Fatherland, has been taken. Having attained all the grades of honor in the city that were permitted by his age, having achieved the highest praise and glory in the discharge of those duties, having governed the *Julian* Forum <note>A political or administrative center in Venice</note> prudently and sacredly, having protected the borders of the Empire with great constancy and marvelous eloquence when there was a controversy about their governance, having served in most honorable embassies, and having managed the *Paduan* Prefecture with incredible wisdom and integrity, nothing else was lacking for his immortal praise except that, after the passage of some years, he should himself recall the memory of the Principate of the best princes, Marcus and Augustinus, his kinsmen: *Behold, death has carried him off! Yet he could never at any time have left this life, nor for a better cause, than by defending the dignity of the Fatherland and by shedding his blood so honorably.* Companions of this fate and participants in his glory were some excellent and most noble ship captains, such as Benedictus Superantius, Catarinus Maripetrus, Vincentius Quirinus, Hieronymus Contarenus, and Marinus Contarenus, in whom the extent of the loss could hardly be explained in words. XX. No one denies that the right of embassy pertains to the free cities of the empire: for they are feudal cities of the Empire, acknowledging only the Caesar as superior, and thence they are called "Free and Imperial Cities, which are subject to no one but the Emperor and the Empire" <note>original: "Freye vnd Reichs-Städte/ so niemand/ als dem Käyser vnd Reiche vnterworffen"</note>: And they are also inserted in the matricula of the Empire, Gail, *Observation 21, number 2*. They bear the same inconveniences as Electors and Princes, in the Recess of the Empire published at Augsburg in the year 1548, § "When also" <note>original: "Wann auch"</note>, Gail, *said observation 21, number 9*. When diets are convened by the Emperor, they have the right of suffrage in them, *Recess of the Empire, Public Audience published in the year 1548, § When also, Gail, said place, number 9*; indeed, they have the first instance in the Imperial Chamber, Gail, *1, observation 17*. And thus, since in this part they enjoy the same privileges and rights as Princes, Gail concludes that one must judge of those cities no differently than of the Prince himself, *2, observation 57, number 3*.

XXI. However, this distinction between the embassies of Princes and other estates of the Empire must be well attended to; that if they send Legates within the limits of the Empire, and indeed to the Emperor or public diets, they are, speaking properly, called not Legates but deputies: yet with the rights and privileges of Legates retained. For the Lord Besold says, Legates are sent to a peer; Deputies to a superior; Commissaries to an inferior. But when they are sent to other Princes of the Empire or to foreign Kings or Republics, they retain both the name and the privileges of Legates.

XXII. However, this caution must be applied, that they be sent away to foreigners in such business as concerns only their own territory. If, however, they were to send Legates to foreigners for causes of the Empire under their own auspices, without the Emperor's knowledge and consent, they would commit the crime of high treason <note>original: "crimen perduellionis"</note>, and would fall into a sin against the Caesarean Majesty, Vayer 6. 7.

XXI. Hoc tamen discrimen Legationum Principum et caterorum Imperii statuum probè attendendum est; quòd si intra Imperii limites et quidem ad Imperatorem, vel Comitia publica Legatos mittant, eos propriè loquendo non Legatos sed deputatos dici: retentis tamen juribus et privilegiis Legatorum. Legati enim, inquit, Dominus Besold. mittuntur ad parem; Deputati ad superiorem; Commissarii ad inferiorem. Cum verò ad alios Principes Imperii vel ad exteros Reges vel Respublicas mittantur, et nomen et privilegia retinent Legatorum.

XXII. Haec autem cautela adhibenda, ut in tali negotio ad exteros ablegentur, quod territorium suum tantum concernit. Si verò propter Imperii causas suis auspiciis inscio et non consentiente Imperatore ad exteros Legatos mitterent, crimen perduellionis committerent, et in Caesaream Maiestatem piaculum inciderent Vayer 6. 7.

EUCHARIUS. Now tell me briefly what should be decided about the Weasel, and how it ought to be named in the common tongue. 

ANONYMOUS. The name of "weasel" is taken in a narrower sense by some writers, and in a broader sense by others. For among the ancients, there are two kinds of weasels: one domestic and common, which is called <term>galē</term> <gloss>weasel</gloss> in Greek; the other kind is wild, which is called <term>iktis</term> <gloss>marten</gloss> in Greek. But the term "weasel" began to be used by later authors not only for the *Gale* and the *Ictis*, but also for the cat, and for the fish that they call the Lamprey, and for the bird that is called <term>weicker</term> <gloss>weaver/finch</gloss> in German. 

EUCHARIUS. Now I desire to know from you how the Latins name Ermines or Hermellas, Wisellas, Mardras, Furos, Iltos, and Frettas. For we use these names commonly now. 

ANONYMOUS. I would prefer that you know this from another. For I see that men, even learned ones, have sweated much over this matter.

It is also established from what has already been said that the Jews held buried animals in aversion, because buried things were a source of horror and disgust, and hence they committed those animals to the earth with a different intention than the Gentiles, since Alexander the Great had a tomb built for his Bucephalus, and Augustus for his horse, out of gratitude, as <term>Pliny</term> is the author in his Natural History, book 8, chapter 42. <term>Jacobus Gutherius</term> asserts that Lucius Verus and Hadrian did the same in his work <term>De Jure Manium</term> <gloss>On the Law of the Spirits of the Dead</gloss>, book 2, chapter 37, and <term>Lilius Gregorius Gyraldus</term> affirms in his book on the various rites of burial that among the Assyrians and Scythians horses were buried with kings. And also, by Civil Law, the use of arms is prohibited to private individuals (*Law 1, Code, On the use of arms; Novella 17, chapter the final; chapter 1, § "Who is a rustic," On keeping the peace, in Feudal uses*). Therefore, what is not allowed to these directly will also not be allowed to others indirectly under the pretext of a Cliental treaty. But if the subjects are not merely private individuals, but the magistrate sustains a person subordinated to a superior, and has been assumed into a share of the cares: then, just as they themselves [are entitled], they are rightly [protected] against unjust force by a Magistrate exceeding his bounds: 1. Because of the office of Magistrate which they hold. 2. Because of the prescription of natural law. 3. Because of the manner of mutual obligation. 4. Because of the Theological axiom that the Gospel does not abolish politics. 5. Because of the testimonies of approved Examples. 6. Because of the consequence of the absurd: to defend themselves (Gerhard, aforementioned place, n. 485; Reinking, aforementioned law, book 1, class 1, c. 5, n. 44 and following). So also, those who are in their clientage can be summoned for their defense. However, it is more humane that the protector is not obligated to defense against a parent and his own blood (*Law: "The laws of blood," Digest, On the Rule of Law; § the last, Institutes, On the succession of agnates and guardians; Law: "Of humanity," 23, Code, On excuses from guardianship*).

### XXIV.

If several persons received into protection by the same party are attacked by outsiders at the same time, the cause of those who are older in protection is stronger (*argument from Law 2, Law: "If the estate," 4, Code, Who is stronger in pledge; Law: "As often as," 98, Digest, On the Rule of Law; argument from Law 9, §4, Digest, On the Publician Action; chapter "He who," extra, On Prebends, in the Sext; chapter "He who is prior," 54, On the Rule of Law, in the Sext*). But if the strength suffices, both must be helped (*argument from Law 49, On optimal legacies*). If one fosters a better cause than the other, equity dictates that the more just cause must be assisted. If they are fighting among themselves, I believe neither should be assisted (from *chapter "Finally," 14, q. 5*).

### XXV.

Moreover, the client is bound by law to reimburse the protector for the expenses made for the defense (*Law: "The works," 21, Digest, On the works of freedmen; argument from Law 33, in the end, On the Administration of Guardians*). And this is true even if the protector has succumbed and been defeated.

the reception of light, which they cannot escape as easily in a way that is convenient, as our opinion is accused of confusion of the faculties. For the formal distinction which we admit between these faculties removes it very well.

§. 24. Philosophers who set out to explain the nature of the intellect consider two things primarily in it: namely, actions and habit. The habit of the intellect, which others call intellectual memory, is nothing other, according to the mind of the Philosopher (<term>Controv. 8, Book 3, On the Soul</term>), than a certain facility born from various acts, by which the intellect perceives things. Most make its actions threefold, according to the threefold mode in which the intellect is occupied about its object. For it either represents the object simply, or it brings forth a judgment about the object represented to it, or it infers one thing from the judged object. The first action they call simple operation, the second judgment, the third discourse. Others, having excluded judgment and discourse from the intellect and left it with only simple apprehension, wish to say that judging or affirming are acts of the will—to which I would assent when I notice that, while I judge, I judge freely, so that finding freedom in my judgment, I would easily conclude that the will must also be in it, since freedom is so essential to the will that it cannot be taken from the will—to these, I say, I would assent, were I not to experience at every moment that the powers I have of judging participate in the intellect. For I cannot deny that I am conscious of those actions while they are being performed, or that I lack knowledge of the object that I am dividing, etc.; for it would be madness to judge what I do not know.

§. 25. Moved by these reasons, I posit this assertion: judgment and discourse participate in the nature of both faculties, namely, intellect and will, and therefore there is a third faculty in me arising from the two others taken jointly, such as the faculty I have of opening and communicating my concepts to others, in which is always found the perception of the mind and the will to reveal to another what we conceive.

§. 26. Simple apprehension is the first operation or thought of the mind, by which we know something without affirmation or negation, or the thought by which we contemplate an image, notion, concept, and idea, and set it before ourselves.

§. 24. Intellectus naturam explicaturi Philosophi, duo imprimis in ipso actiones scilicet et habitum considerant. Intellectus habitus, quem alii memoriam intellectualem vocant, nihil aliud est secundum mentem Philosophi *Controv. 8. lib. 3. de anima*, præter facilitatem quandam ex variis actibus ortam, quâ intellectus res percipit. Triplices verò ejus actiones plerique faciunt pro triplici modo quo intellectus circa suum objectum versatur. Vel enim objectum simpliciter repræsentat, vel judicium de objecto sibi repræsentato profert, vel aliud ex objecto judicato infert. Primam actionem, simplicem operationem, secundam judicium, tertiam discursum vocant. Alii seclusis ab intellectu, judicio et discursu, eique solâ relictâ simplici apprehensione, judicare seu affirmare volunt esse actus voluntatis, quibus assentirer, cùm animadvertam, me, dum judico, liberè judicare, ita ut libertatem in meo judicio reperiens, voluntatem ei etiam inesse debere facilè concludam, quandoquidem libertas adeò sit voluntati essentialis, ut à voluntate tolli non possit, his inquam, assentirer, ni singulis momentis potentias quas habeo judicandi de intellectu participare, experirer. §. 29. Universaliter non valere dixi: Non dubium enim quin à sensibus etiam aliquas species intellectus hauriat. Verissimum namque quod annotat Dominus la Forge omnes nostras ideas à quatuor differentibus causis excitari, actione scilicet sensuum, vestigiis memoriæ, actione spirituum animalium à corde ad cerebrum ascendentium, et denique ab ipsa mente se ad cogitandum determinante. A sensibus hoc modo excitari communis est Philosophorum opinio. Objectum nempe sensuum externorum veluti fores primò propellit. per hos introductum ingerit sese in sensum internum seu materialem phantasiam; hâc deinde crassiori objecti specie excitatus intellectus illapsum in sensum internum objectum, protinus apprehendit, ejusque expressionem in animo effingit.

§. 30. Sensuum autem, quos in me deprehendo, naturam si inspiciam, negare non possum, eos quoque aliam esse hujus quam habeo percipiendi potentiæ speciem; Nam quamvis sentire aut imaginari non possim sine corpore, actio tamen illa mentis, quâ sensationis aut imaginationis conscius sum, est planè spiritualis et incorporea. Definiuntur itaque perceptiones, quibus motus à corpore aliquo objecto fibrillis nervorum impressus et in cerebrum delatus, ac sensorio communi mediantibus spiritibus animalibus, ventriculis cerebri contentis, communicatus, à mente in sensorio communi percipitur; ita ut rectè tres hi in sentiendo gradus ponantur: motus organi, mentis cogitatio, et voluntatis determinatio. *Vide Dominum la Chambre in Characteribus passionum de natura doloris. pagina 215. et sequentes* ubi sensationem, cognitionem seu perceptionem esse evincit.

### LXII.

Quod si uero cum eiusmodi certamen susceptum sit, qui praeter diuinam Scripturam, sanctorum Patrum quoque, et uniuersalis Ecclesiae autoritatem non recuset, nullum extat, quod eadem ratione probari non ualeat.

### LXIII.

Ceterum Theologiae munus, non id solum est, quod modo exposuimus, nempe principia sua contra negantes, aut impugnantes defendere, aliasque et alias conclusiones, quae ad rem Christianam tuendam et illustrandam faciant, rationis ui inde colligere: uerum etiam internis externisque scientiae huius praesidiis, et adminiculis adhibitis, ualide utrumque communire.

### LXIIII.

Interna et propria Theologiae praesidia eas rationes appellamus, quae petuntur ex Scriptura Canonica: ex fida Christi et Apostolorum traditione: ex Catholica et Apostolicae Ecclesiae autoritate, ex Conciliorum generalium, Romanorumque Pontificum Canonibus: ex ueterum denique et recentiorum Patrum, Theologorumque monumentis.

### LXV.

<margin>+</margin> Externa, et quasi ex alieno fundo emendicata, ea dici possunt, quae sumuntur ex naturalium Philosophorum placitis, ex Iureconsultorum responsis: nam et ipsi quoque inter uerae Philosophiae Professores censeri uolunt: ex rerum gestarum commentariis: ex ipsis demum humanae rationis opibus.

### LXVI.

Etenim cum duplex sit argumentandi genus: alterum autoritate nitens Theologo proprium, alterum ratione instructum Philosopho peculiare, si priori et proprio uti non datur, quod priori proximum est Theologus arripiens, pro autoritate, ratione se defendit: saepe tamen utrumque probandi genus simul coniungit.

### LXVII.

Hinc patet stultam eorum esse sapientiam, qui de Theologico quopiam argumento uerba facturi, Patrum, Conciliorum, et Scripturarum autoritate, ueluti parum firma repudiata, ratiunculis tantum ex naturali Philosophia emendicatis, disceptant. Non enim intelligunt μωρόσοφοι illi,

Porro autem inter interna Theologiae praesidia hoc interest: quod argumenta ex sacrarum literarum autoritate, Catholicaeque et Apostolicae Ecclesiae definitione, et perpetua constantique eiusdem Ecclesiae traditione ducta, non solum sint propria et interna, uerum etiam necessaria: Sumpta uero ex Sancti, uel Patris cuiuspiam doctrina, cuiuscunque demum ordinis, sanctitatis, uel autoritatis extiterit, probabiliter tantum concludunt. Temerarium tamen esset, a plurium Sanctorum P. iudicio, praesertim in Scripturarum interpretatione, longius recedere.

### LXIX.

Grauiter proinde et periculose errare conuincuntur, qui D. Hieronymum testamentariarum Scripturarum regulam facientes, illos tantum libros inter Canonicos haberi uolunt, quibus idem Pater aliud fortassis agens, Canonicorum nomen alicubi imponit.

### LV.

You will say that none of these things surpasses the sense of reason, and that in such a way, even if they are sometimes false, they can nevertheless be held as true; but the mysteries of faith, from which the Theologian weaves his argumentation, exceed all sense and all thought of the mind by a great deal.

### LVI.

Let it be so; but it had to be so, especially in those matters which are believed concerning God without evidence of reason. For since God, the Best and Greatest <note>original: "Opt. Max." (Optimus Maximus)</note>, surpasses all reason and exists above all nature and thought, it was necessary that many things should pertain to Him which would exceed the grasp of the human mind; for such a great thing cannot be comprehended by the narrowness of our intellect.

### LVII.

But if the works of God could be comprehended by human reason, and if what and how great He Himself is could be understood by us, God would surely not truly be God; for everything that our intellect can grasp of God by itself is very narrow and infinitely less than the divine majesty.

### LVIII.

Yet it is not because they are of such a kind that they should therefore be held as vain or unworthy of faith. For all and each are most worthy of faith, as they have been received long ago not only by the unanimous consent of the entire Catholic and Apostolic Church, which is the pillar and foundation of truth, and approved by its long and constant use, but also often confirmed by many and great miracles.

### LIX.

Among which, certainly, one should not consider it a minor thing that twelve men of humble lot, destitute of all human wisdom and power, could persuade the wise of the age, and those given over to belly and flesh, of those things from which the common judgment of men mostly shrinks.

### LX.

For what is more alien to human sense than to worship a man who was put on a cross? And for the sake of His worship and love, to regard life, all fortunes, and all the conveniences of this world as nothing? To regard hunger, thirst, cold, and the utmost poverty of all things in place of the greatest delights? To pour forth ardent prayers for those who persecute and slander? To show oneself joyful in adversities and sad in prosperity? etc.

### LXI.

### LV.

Dices nihil horum omnium rationis sensum superare, atque ita, ut falsa quandoque sint, pro ueris tamen haberi posse: fidei uero mysteria, ex quibus Theologus argumentationem texit, omnem omnino sensum, omnemque mentis cogitationem plurimum excedere.

### LVI.

Sit ita: at ita esse debuit, in ijs praesertim, quae de Deo citra rationis euidentiam creduntur. Nam cum Deus Opt. Max. rationem omnem superet, supraque omnem naturam, et cogitationem existat, necessum fuit, ut multa ei conuenirent, quae humanae mentis captum excederent: nostri enim intellectus angustiis tanta res comprehendi non potest.

### LVII.

Quod si humana ratione Dei opera comprehendi, qualisque et quantus esset ipse, a nobis intelligi posset, Deus profecto uere Deus non esset: perangustum est enim omne illud, et diuina maiestate infinitis partibus minus, quod intellectus noster, de Deo per se capere potest.

### LVIII.

Neque tamen quia eiusmodi sunt isthaec, ideo etiam pro uanis, aut fide indignis habenda sunt: sunt enim omnia et singula fide dignissima, utpote non solum unanimi totius Catholicae et Apostolicae Ecclesiae, quae columna et firmamentum ueritatis est, consensione iam olim recepta, longoque et constanti eiusdem usu approbata, uerum etiam multis saepe, et magnis rerum miraculis confirmata.

### LIX.

Inter quae sane non pro minimo habendum est, duodecim abiectae sortis homines, omni humana sapientia, et potentia destitutos, ea saeculi sapientibus, uentrique et carni deditis hominibus persuadere potuisse, a quibus commune hominum iudicium abhorret maxime.

### LX.

Ecquid enim ab humano sensu alienius, quam hominem in crucem actum adorare? praeque illius unius cultu, et amore uitam, fortunasque omnes, et omnia mundi huius commoda flocci facere? famem, sitim, frigus, summamque rerum omnium egestatem, summarum delitiarum loco habere? pro persequentibus et calumniantibus ardentes preces fundere? in aduersis laetum, in prosperis tristem sese praebere? etc.

In infinitum igitur distant, ut essentia ita & persona finita & infinita: Essentia finita est individua ob unitatem & incommunicabilis ad plures personas ob finitatem: Infinita vel licet sit summe individua ob summam unitatem, tamen vere est communicabilis ad plures personas ob infinitatem. In finitis persona una distinguitur ab altera non minus essendi singularitate, quàm subsistendi incommunicabilitate: At in mysterio <term>Trinitatis</term> personae distinguuntur ab invicem subsistendi saltim incommunicabilitate, non vero essentiae singularitate, una non est altera, ejusdem tamen est cum altera essentiae numericae. Illic persona quaevis tota distincta est ab alia persona & separata, nullamque habent intrinsecam connexionem: Heic tametsi personae distinguantur realiter, non tamen possunt separari in esse, sed ejus ratione una est in altera, nec esse potest extra alteram ob essentiae identitatem. And yet, properly speaking, <term>to intelligens</term> <gloss>the intelligent</gloss> is not the difference of a person, for in these things, as transcendents, genus and difference do not have a place, nor does it pertain to the formal reason of a person, but to the material, in that a person formally agrees with a subject. The formal of a person is <term>authyparxia</term> <gloss>self-existence</gloss> and the incommunicability of subsistence, that is, the ultimate reason of subsisting, and independence in subsisting, by the force of which a nature is ultimately actuated in the reason of subsisting, and cannot be united with another and communicated in such a way that it receives the reason of subsisting from it, or is actuated and completed further by it. This formal reason of a person is expressed by two terms, of which one is *positive*, <term>authyparxia</term>, because a person and a subject is <term>authyparkton</term> <gloss>self-subsisting</gloss> and <term>idiosystaton</term> <gloss>self-constituted</gloss>, terminated by a proper personality. The other is *negative*, incommunicable in subsisting, so that communication with another subject or person, by which it might be terminated and completed further, is denied: for thus it would not subsist by the most perfect reason if it could be communicated in such a way, and thus the aptitude of depending on something sustaining is excluded, since that is repugnant to the reason of a person.

Senis illa fuit conditio, quem inveteratâ apud Caesarem gratiâ super caeteros amicos meminimus aliàs floruisse. Qui igitur mirum sit, si Filii multum deteriore loco fuerunt? It is not my place to settle the dispute between such great men, nor to pronounce the judgment of a judge, as I see Spanheim had once intended to assume those parts with prudent counsel. **XX V.** Ad alterum genus intellectionum pertinet enunciatio mentalis, quam, ut Recentiores distinguant à propositione, etiam ad tertiam mentis operationem spectante, et virtualem discursum includente, rectè definiunt, judicium immediatum de re aliqua: id est tale, quod praedicatum de subiecto affirmat propter connexionem inter ipsummet subiectum et praedicatum. Cùm è contrà omnis discursus sit judicium mediatum, quia mediatè approbat connexionem praedicati cum subiecto. Potissima horum actuum proprietas est veritas formalis, quae nihil est aliud, quam conformitas judicij cum obiecto, sicut econtrà falsitas est difformitas judicij cum obiecto; ut proinde judicium verum sit illud, quod enunciat obiectum ita se habere, sicut à parte rei se habet: falsum illud, si obiectum non ita se habet, sicut ipsum enunciat.

**XX VI.** Enunciatio semel vera nunquam potest transire in falsam, nec vicissim falsa in veram; cognitio enim eadem, semper idem repraesentat, ergo cognitio, quae cum veritate repraesentavit Adamum scribere, pro hoc instanti, quod copula verbalis designavit, repraesentavit in aeternum Adamum scribere hoc instanti. Sicut enim impossibile est Adamum scripsisse hoc instanti A, et non scripsisse hoc instanti A, ita impossibile est, ut cognitio quae verè repraesentat illum hoc instanti A scripsisse, aliquando repraesentet illum non scripsisse: cum propositio in aeternum tantùm de hoc, et de nullo alio instanti loquatur. De falsitate pari modo discurrendum est, quod si propositio repraesentaret aliud tempus ab illo, quod primò repraesentârat, hoc ipso non eadem, sed alia et nova esset repraesentatio, et consequenter nova cognitio.

**XX VII.** Ad tertium et primarium genus operationum humani intellectûs spectat discursus formalis, sive syllogismus; qui est oratio, in qua quibusdam positis, aliud quiddam, ab his, quae posita sunt, necessario accidit, eò quod haec sunt. Et essentialiter non tantùm conclusionem, sed ipsas etiam praemissas involuit, nec ullus censetur condidisse syllogismum formalem, qui vel aliquid infert sine ullis praemissis, vel factis praemissis nihil infert. Ut autem assensus conclusionis ab alio assensu immediatè judicativo dignosci possit, debet intrinsecè attingere obiectum praemissarum tanquam motivum, et rationem formalem assentiendi. Quod inde probatur, quia omnis actus tendens in aliquod obiectum materiale propter aliud formale, debet attingere illud obiectum formale: atqui motivum formale conclusionis quà talis est obiectum Praemissarum, sive identitas extremorum cum medio tertio, ergo debet actus conclusionis, quà talis, illud obiectum attingere. Confirmatur; quia nisi actus conclusionis attingat iterum motivum formale, in aliquibus syllogismis non poterit dari ratio, cur haec propositio potiùs sit conclusio, quàm alia ex tribus, quaelibet enim illarum potest per modum conclusionis ex alijs inferri.

**XX VIII.** Praeter objectum conclusionis, et obiectum praemissarum debet ab actu couclusionis etiam attingi bonitas illationis, quae est identitas inter obiectum praemissarum et obiectum conclusionis: nam etiam haec bonitas est partiale motivum, quod una cum obiecto praemissarum intellectum movet ad inferendam conclusionem; ablata enim hâc unicâ connexione inter obiectum praemissarum et obiectum con-

clusionis, quantumuis maneat obiectum præmissarum, intellectus non moueretur ad conclusionem. Sicuti ergo, cum medicinam amamus propter sanitatem, etiam amamus connexionem, quam habet medicina cum sanitate reparanda, quia seclusâ hac connexione medicinam non amaremus, ita etiam intellectus, vt possit moueri ad concludendum, non debet tantùm attingere obiectum præmissarum, sed etiam bonitatem illationis.

XXIX. Dubitant quidam num judicium de bonitate illationis debeat esse actus distinctus et intermedius, inter assensum præmissarum, et assensum conclusionis, per quem intellectus reflexè cognoscat hanc conclusionem ritè inferri ex his præmissis, eò quòd illa sint identificata inter se, quæ sunt identificata uni tertio. Nos probabiliùs existimamus, *judicium de bonitate illationis ab actu conclusionis distinctum non necessariò semper requiri*, maximè in hominibus exercitatis, quibus clarissimè notum est principium illud, *quæcunque sunt eadem uni tertio, etc.* Nam tales postquam in præmissis viderunt, extrema conclusionis esse identificata uni tertio, immediatè conclusionis actum inferunt, qui simul et semel et obiectum præmissarum, et bonitatem illationis, et obiectum conclusionis attingit. In iis tamen hominibus, qui in faciendis syllogismis exercitati non sunt, quique etiam, postquam viderunt, duo esse identificata uni tertio, adhuc dubitare possunt, an illa duo sint identificata inter se, omnino *sequi putamus judicium de bonitate illationis distinctum, et ipsam conclusionem præcedens*: tam imperfectus enim horum intellectus non est sufficienter determinatus per obiectum præmissarum ad conclusionem sine ulla hæsitatione inferendam.

# *Operationes Voluntatis humanæ.*

XXX. Voluntatem esse virtutem spiritualem liberam, obiecti appetitiuam, certum est apud omnes: eandem nec ab intellectu, nec ab anima distingui, supra thesi tertia insinuauimus. *Obiectum materiale*, circa quod illa versatur, est omne id, quod intellectus sub ratione boni vel mali cognoscere potest. *Obiectum formale*, siue illud, quod immediatè voluntatem mouet, est bonum et malum, prius mouet ad actus prosecutionis; posteriùs ad actus fugæ. Bonum, quod voluntatem mouet, triplex est: *honestum, delectabile, utile*. Nullum ex his voluntatem allicere potest, nisi priùs sit cognitum: ipsa tamen cognitio non est motiuum voluntatis, sed mera conditio applicans motiuum. *Malum ut malum*, siue tantùm sub ratione mali propositum, voluntas amare non potest, secùs si sub ratione boni saltem apparentis obijciatur.

Ordinariè loquendo, vt aliquod bonum nobis ipsis amemus, et appetamus, sufficit cognoscere illud bonum esse nobis conueniens; nec opus est, vt in nobis ipsis aliquam bonitatem agnoscamus, propter quam digni simus, vt nobis tale bonum amemus. Si verò alteri personæ amamus, aut cupimus aliquod bonum, requiritur, vt in illa apprehendamus aliquam bonitatem, propter quam illam tali bono dignam æstimamus. ### XXII.
The human intellect, as it is distinguished from the angelic, is a spiritual cognitive virtue, requiring for some state at least to operate dependently upon a <term>phantasm</term> <gloss>sensory image</gloss>: it is not really distinguished from the soul, and in one man it is unique; yet it bears various names according to the variety of its operations. Its object is being taken in its whole breadth, as it includes uncreated and created being, natural and supernatural, positive and negative, real and rational being: for we experience that we are occupied with all these in our intellect, whether clearly or obscurely, or through proper or alien <term>species</term>. The operations of this power are those vital acts by which a man is formally and intrinsically rendered intelligent.

### XXIII.
Intellection (the same, indeed an even greater reason exists for volition) consists formally in a quality identified with the action by the soul that depends on it; and thus it is a modal entity, which is not only immediately united to the soul by itself, but also proceeds from it without an intermediate action distinct from the entity of intellection itself. The reason is that a free act, for example love, is intrinsically and in itself free; yet nothing is free formally, intrinsically, and in itself except the formal exercise itself or the free determination of the will by which it applies itself freely to this object and flees another. This determination, however, cannot be anything other than a free action producing love: therefore, so that love may be free in itself and intrinsically, it must have its production identified with itself. We feel the same about intellection; for this is not an image of an object that is just any kind or dead, as a wooden statue of Caesar is, but is a living representation and an actual attention of the soul; which seems to be able to be understood as little without the effort and action of the soul itself as the former, therefore the vital image of the object must have the productive action itself identified with itself: for intellection is also the exercise of the intellect, just as love is the exercise of the will.

### XXIV.
The intellections of man are for the most part revoked to three genera: namely, apprehension, judgment or enunciation, and discourse. Apprehension is an act of the intellect that represents an object in a simple way, affirming or denying nothing about it. Concerning this genus of acts, many difficulties occur through philosophy, and we propose one: namely, whether the human intellect can objectively prescind <gloss>abstract or separate</gloss> between formalities identified in an object, that is, attaining one while not attaining the others? We judge it more probable that it implies a contradiction in created things for acts of the intellect to objectively prescind. The reason is because if, for example, animality could be known in man without knowing rationality, then the same indivisible thing could be known and not known; these are no less contradictory than being produced and not being produced, existing and not existing; which, since they cannot be verified of one and the same created thing according to all, one and the same thing will not be able to be known and not known. More correctly, therefore, a virtue of formally prescinding is granted to the intellect, such that the act elicited through it attains all formalities identified in the object at all, yet with this distinction: that it knows one clearly, others confusedly, or in such a way that by the force of that cognition it cannot give an account of what kind they were.
