### XXII.
Intellectus humanus prout diſtinguitur ab angelico , eſt virtus cognoſcitiva ſpiritualis , exigens pro aliquo ſaltem ſtatu dependenter à phantaſmate operari : is realiter ab anima non diſtinguitur , & in vno homine vnicus eſt ; pro varietate tamen operationum varia nomina ſortitur. Eius obiectum eſt ens in tota ſua latitudine ſumptum , prout nimirum includit ens increatum & creatum , naturale & ſupernaturale , poſitivum & negativum , ens reale & rationis : experimur enim , nos circa hæc omnia intellectu verſari , vel clarè , vel obſcurè , vel per ſpecies proprias vel alienas. Operationes huius potentiæ ſunt illi actus vitales , per quos homo formaliter & intrinſecè redditur intelligens.

### XXIII.
Intellectio ( par , imò maior eſt ratio de volitione ) conſiſtit formaliter in qualitate per actionem ſecum identificatam ab anima dependente , adeoque eſt entitas modalis , quæ non tantùm animæ immediatè per ſe vnitur , ſed etiam ab eadem ſine actione intermedia , ab ipſa entitate intellectionis diſtincta , procedit. Ratio eſt quia actus liber , verbi gratia amor , eſt intrinſecè , & in ſe , liber , atqui nihil eſt liberum formaliter intrinſecè , & in ſe , niſi ipſum formale exercitium ſeu ipſa libera determinatio voluntatis , per quam ſe liberè huic obiecto applicat , ab alio fugit. Hæc autem determinatio non poteſt aliquid aliud eſſe , quàm libera actio productiva amoris : ergo ut amor ſit in ſe , & intrinſecè liber , debet habere ſecum identificatam ſui productionem. Quod ipſum de intellectione ſentimus ; hæc enim eſt imago obiecti non qualiscunque & emortua , vti eſt ſtatua lignea Cæſaris , ſed eſt viva repræſentatio , & actualis animæ attentio ; quod tam parùm ſine ipſius animæ conatu , & actione intelligi poſſe videtur , quàm prius , ergo imago vitalis obiecti debet ſecum habere identificatam ipſam actionem productivam : nam etiam intellectio eſt ipſum exercitium intellectûs , ſicut amor eſt exercitium voluntatis.

### XXIV.
Intellectiones hominis ferè ad tria genera revocantur : videlicet apprehenſionem , iudicium ſeu enuntiationem , & diſcurſum. Apprehenſio eſt actus intellectûs , qui ſimplici quodam modo repræſentat obiectum , nihil de eo affirmando , vel negando. Circa hoc genus actuum plures per Philoſophiam occurrunt difficultates , nos vnam proponimus : An ſcilicet intellectus humanus inter formalitates in obiecto identificatas præſcindere obiectivè poſſit , vnam ſcilicet attingendo , alias verò non attingendo ? Probabiliùs iudicamus , implicare in rebus creatis actus intellectûs obiectivè præſcindentes. Ratio eſt , quia ſi verbi gratia in homine cognoſci poſſet animalitas non cognitâ rationalitate , tum eadem indiviſibilis res poſſet cognoſci , & non cognoſci , hæc non ſunt minus contradictoria , quàm produci & non produci , exiſtere & non exiſtere ; quæ cum iuxta omnes de vna eademque re creata verificari non poſſint , non etiam poterit vna & eadem res cognoſci , & non cognoſci. Rectiùs itaque conceditur intellectui Virtus formaliter præſcindendi , ita , vt actus per illum elicitus omnes omnino formalitates in obiecto identificatas attingat , cum hoc tamen diſcrimine , quod vnam cognoſcat clarè , alias confuſè , ſive ita , vt vi illius cognitionis non poſſit rationem reddere quales fuerint.

XXXII. Actus voluntatis sunt multiplices. Primaria illorum praerogatiua est, quod soli illi possint esse formaliter, et intrinsece liberi. Est autem libertas duplex: vna in actu primo, quae potentiae, altera in actu secundo, quae operationi competit. Libertas in actu primo est potentia libera, siue talis, quae, positis omnibus ad agendum requisitis, potest agere et non agere: libertas in actu secundo est ipsa operatio, quae ita procedit a suo principio, vt positis omnibus requisitis potuerit non procedere, adeoque; cuius negatio potest coniungi cum principio proximo et adaequato, in actu primo completo. Pro utriusque definitionis ampliore declaratione; aduerto primo: nomine praerequisitorum ad actum secundum intelligi ex parte Dei concursum indifferentem paratum, ne impediatur creatura, quo minus se pro arbitratu ad quemcunque effectum extendere possit. Ex parte obiecti adesse debet repraesentatio indifferens tam sub ratione boni, quam sub ratione mali, aut saltem molesti. Ex parte creaturae, potentia expedita, et immunis ab omnibus impedimentis, et insuper absentia omnis principij, quod ita necessario secum trahit effectum, vt cum contrario, vel negatione illius effectus potentia proxima coniungi non possit. Secundum: potentiam liberam debere pro arbitratu simul (simultate potentiae) posse agere et non agere, non in sensu diuiso, sed in sensu composito, hoc est, posito quod omnia requisita ad agendum adsint, non vero in sensu diuiso tantum, hoc est ita, vt agere quidem possit, cum adsint omnia requisita ex parte actus primi, non autem possit agere, si vel vnicum ex requisitis desit. Nam etiam agentia necessaria, quando omnia adsunt, possunt agere, si vnum desit, non possunt agere: vt ergo agentia libera ab his discernantur, debent illa etiam in praesentia omnium requisitorum actionem posse omittere.

XXXIII. Libertas in actu primo subdiuiditur in libertatem contradictionis, siue quoad exercitium, et in libertatem contrarietatis, siue quoad specificationem. Prior est ad actus contradictorios, vt amare et non amare, velle et non velle. Libertas contrarietatis est ad actus contrarios <term>verbi gratia</term> amorem et odium. Rem exemplo declaramus. Deus <term>verbi gratia</term> vt summe bonus proponitur per intellectum voluntati vt amandus, cum aliqua tamen molestia in exercitio amoris subeunda. Vi huius cognitionis voluntas tantum libera est libertate contradictionis, vel ad ponendum, vel ad omittendum actum amoris. Quod si accedat alia cognitio repraesentans etiam seueritatem ipsius Dei in puniendis hominum peccatis, vel aliam rationem, mali speciem, licet falso, praeferentem, fiet voluntas libera etiam libertate contrarietatis: quia posita tali repraesentatione (modo etiam alia requisita adsint) voluntas non tantum amare potest et non amare, sed etiam actum odij amori contrarium elicere.

For although so many illustrious merits to the literary world fought for you, <term>Philippe de Commines</term>, you could not be untouched by this evil. But your virtues finally asserted you and snatched you from prison. They dissipated the storms and tempests of the envious, who were plotting your death for the crime of levity and perfidy falsely fabricated against you. Nor could your own most ample merits, <term>Francis Bacon of Verulam</term>, conferred upon the literary Republic, overcome the envy of other learned men, who strove to undermine your fortune with most acute weapons, the light and fame of which, however, they could not extinguish. I will now refrain from adding more prolixly the dog-like custom of certain men, who, since they can infest the fame of ingenuous men by no other means, do not deem it inhuman to attack it with slanderous barking. I will not inquire, O most distinguished <term>Budé</term>, into the goads by which you were often pierced by the mouths of the malignant, nor will I repeat the wagonloads of injuries cast upon your most skillful and eternally worthy works. It is shameful to remember the impudence that more than once desired that learned men, the lights of the century, be condemned under the guise of other crimes. Finally, may that most execrable crime, most unworthy of the memory of man, remain—by which the <term>Chinese</term>, once moved by the calumny of a certain envious philosopher <term>Lissui</term>, did not refrain from most shamefully destroying all the books of all the learned men with flames. For although discussions may seem truly named as such because truth was thought to be, as it were, purified through them, yet such excessive self-confidence has settled in the minds of some that, thinking nothing right unless it conforms to their own sayings, they are accustomed to move quarrels over any matter whatsoever, and to measure their outcome not so much by the investigation of truth as by the victory of the adversary. <header>OF THE RATIONAL SOUL.</header>

# ERROR XIII.

## That the Rational Soul is transformed into a demon or a brute.

There was a heresy that asserted that the souls of wicked men were converted after death into demons, or into whatever brute animals were appropriate to their merits, as witness Saint Augustine in Book 9, *On the City of God*, chapter 11. Plato taught that the souls of men are demons, and that they become *Lares* <gloss>household spirits</gloss> from men if they are of good merit, but *Lemures* <gloss>restless spirits</gloss> or *Larvae* <gloss>ghosts</gloss> if they are evil. Saint Augustine, in his book *On Heresies* to Quodvultdeus, attributes this error also to Tertullian.

# CORRECTION.

I. This most foolish opinion opens the way to great crimes, for however wicked men have been, whether they imagine themselves becoming ghosts or "Divine Spirits," they become all the worse the more desirous they are of doing harm, to the point that they imagine themselves to be invited after death by certain sacrifices, as if by divine honors, so that they may do harm. And certainly, if the Rational Soul were converted into a demon or a beast, then the soul would cease to be what it was before; for whatever is naturally converted into another thing perishes in order to be turned into the other, just as when wine passes into vinegar, the wine ceases to be what it was before, whence the Rational Soul would be mortal and corruptible, which, however, Tertullian himself denied, as Saint Augustine bears witness.

II. When, however, it is said in John 8, "You are from your father the Devil," and Saint John the Baptist in Matthew 3 called the Jews "a brood of vipers," these were only metaphorical expressions, just as Scripture called Christ a "Lion" and a "Lamb," certainly not in reality, but from a certain similarity, because each had something similar: just as vipers are born devouring their mothers, so the Jews, after they had killed their fathers, namely the Prophets, now wishing to do penance, desired to be born spiritually.

III. Nor did Christ wish the Jews to be children of the devil by nature, but regarding their morals, in which children are accustomed to imitate their parents. Hence he also said to them, "If you are the Children of Abraham, do the works of Abraham." Since therefore Christ will one day say to the reprobate, "Go, you cursed, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels," as is held in Matthew 25, a manifest difference is indicated between the souls of evil men and the demons themselves. And in Wisdom 11, it is said that God preserves souls. How would he preserve them if he converted them into demons?

## Animam Rationalem mutari in Daemonem vel brutum.

Haeresis erat, quae asserebat, animas hominum sceleratorum post mor-

I. Magnis haec opinio stultissima sceleribus viam pandit, quandoqui-

etiam quibusdam sacrificiis, tanquam diuinis honoribus post mortem se inui-
tari opinentur, vt noceant; Et certè si anima Rationalis in daemonem vel pe-

gnum, vtique non verum, sed ex quadam similitudine, eò quod vtrique simile
quid habuerit: ita sicut viperae deuorantes matres suas nascuntur, sic Iudaei
postquam illi Patres suos, Prophetas nimirum occiderant, nunc poeniten-

Therefore, just as that complexion is cold and moist, it claims for itself a cause of this kind, which all natural philosophers affirm to be the star of the Moon, which has a greater convenience with that complexion than the other planets. For as astronomers write, the Moon has the power to cause humidity, because with its rising the waters increase, and with its descent they are diminished. And this water has some coldness admixed with it, just as that complexion does. This complexion occurs when a mixture is composed of the four elements or humors where the humor of water predominates over the others, and it is assimilated to water and winter. Therefore, the phlegmatic are cold and moist. And its signs, by which it ought to be known as the natural philosophers write, are these: that he is fat in the face, white, and sleepy. He has white skin because the phlegmatic is cold, having little blood. Coldness, however, is the mother of whiteness, and he has a fat body because of humidity, and he is lazy because he is heavy, on account of being moist, because every moist thing is heavy. He is fond of sleep on account of the humor ascending to the head, constricting it and individual limbs, because sleep is a binding of the senses. And he also easily receives knowledge and quickly loses it because of humidity, because the moist is fluid. And he rarely goes bald, is always timid and ignorant. And he is fleshy, having small bones in respect to the flesh in his quantity, because he lacks the heat that would wither him. And he is not quickly angered on account of coldness, and he has soft and straight hair because of humidity. And commonly he has watery eyes, and they are unstable like the Moon, having one eye larger than the other, or commonly they have a defect of the eyes. And they are very potent with women and little desiring because of coldness, but because of humidity, they emit much seed. But if certain medicines promote this, they seem to do so by accident, while they either de-obstruct the pores or render the blood more turgid or even more fluid, of which there is more in the following thesis.

## VII.

**O**f the same flour are those sesquipedalian <note>i.e., long-winded, literally "foot-and-a-half-long"</note> words and vain boastings, when they brag of such a medicine by which a wound can be perfectly consolidated in the space of three days, when, however, it is not even possible to provide flesh-generating medicines. Who, I ask, ever saw flesh fashioned by a medicine or generated from a remedy? Trifles! All solid parts are from milk; if the blood abounds with this and distributes it freely through the wounded part, the wound will be healed shortly. But if it has been contaminated by an acid intemperance, or a saline one, or by a perverse mixture, healing will be a slow work. Indeed, consolidation will be awaited in vain unless first the acid is broken, or the sharp salt is tempered, or the legitimate mixture of the blood is restored. By what remedies we may achieve this, this is the task, this is the labor. For the praises of practitioners do not satisfy, as if the blood, by the help of wound-medicines adorned with some peculiar virtue for this business, were disposed in such a way that from it apt and praiseworthy flesh and every other lost substance could be promptly restored. For as long as that peculiar virtue cannot be explained, as it is in fact inexplicable to them, so long does that matter remain in an ambiguous and slippery state. And since we have noted a triple vicious state of the blood, how will it be possible to whitewash three walls with this one bucket? The most famous Craan very well chastises this error and lashes out at the perverse and irrational use of wound-decoctions. For since even the smallest

## VII.

**S**imilis farinae sunt sesquipedalia illa verba & vanae gloriationes, dum ejusmodi jactant medicamentum, quo vulnus spatio tridui perfecte consolidari possit, cum tamen ne quidem dari queant medicamenta carnem generantia : Ecquis quaeso unquam vidit carnem a medicamento fabrefactam vel ex remedio generatam ? Nugae ! Omnes partes solidae sunt ex lacte, quo si sanguis abundet idque per partem sauciatam libere dispenset, vulnus brevi sanabitur. Sin vero intemperie acida, aut salina aut perversa mixtione fuerit contaminatus, lentum opus erit sanatio. Imo frustra expectabitur consolidatio, nisi prius vel infringatur acidum : aut sal acre temperetur, aut legitima sanguinis mixtura restituatur. Quibus vero remediis id assequamur, hoc opus hic labor est. Neque enim satisfaciunt practicorum elogia, quasi sanguis ope vulnerariorum peculiari quadam virtute ad hoc negotium exornatorum ita disponatur, ut ex eo apta & laudabilis caro quaevisque alia substantia deperdita promte restitui possit : Quamdiu enim peculiaris illa virtus explicari nequit, sicut revera apud illos inexplicabilis est, tamdiu res ista versatur in ambiguo & lubrico. Et cum triplicem sanguinis statum vitiosum notaverimus, quomodo una hac fidelia tres dealbari poterunt parietes ? ### Quæstio Sexta.

§. 11. *An si Christus post Ascensionem esset in terris, non esset noster Sacerdos?*

In Epistola ad Hebr. cap. 8. vers. 4. hæc legere est verba: *Si enim esset super terram, nec esset Sacerdos*: Ex his adversarii <unclear>furtim</unclear> colligunt, Christum corpore suo in cœlis versari et non esse in terris: Nostrum igitur est Herculi clavam extorquere et solide respondere: *primum illud*: Si Christus Sacerdos esse non posset, (si esset in terris) consequeretur, eum, cum in terris conversaretur, et in crucis ara Patri suo se offerret, et 40. diebus discipulis suis multis argumentis ostenderet, non fuisse sacerdotem. Consequens est absurdum. Ergo et antecedens. Connexi ratio in propatulo est, quia tum in terris fuit. *Secundò illud*: Si Christus, quia Sacerdos, non esset in terris, quà Deus Sacerdos non esset (quia semper ut in cœlo, ita in terra est) Posterius absurdum, ex confessione adversæ partis. Ergo et prius. *Tertium isthoc*: Si Christus quia Sacerdos, non esset in terris, secundum humanam naturam non esset Sacerdos, quia secundum eam, fatentibus illis, est in Cœlis. Posterius absurdum, quia Sacerdotium ad ipsius pertinet officium, adeoque utramque Naturam. Ergo et prius. *Denique* et *hoc*, Si in terris non esset, Sacerdos æternus non esset, quia in novissimo die de Cœlo rediturus est. Falsum hoc, Ergo et illud. Mirum ergo est adversarios huic loco, tanquam tibicini aut suggrundæ alicui ædificium suæ opinionis suffulcire: Verùm enim verò per cuniculos rem agunt. Nam 1. textui inferunt verba, *secundum humanam naturam*, 2. verba accipiunt de alterutra Christi natura, cum Epistola loquatur de toto Christo. Move jam rotam Syllogisticam, quid exibit? annon isthoc?

## Fifth Question.

### *§. 10. Into what kind of Heaven did Christ ascend?*

The Pontificians make the heaven a corporeal one, and believe that Christ ascended into it, whether he remains within this Heaven itself or whether he remains above and outside all the Heavens, such that he touches the convex part of the highest Heaven with his feet (Bellarmine, *Book 3 on the Incarnation of the Word, chapter 12*). If that were the case, Christ would not be said to have ascended "above all the heavens" (Ephesians 4, verse 10), to have "penetrated the heavens" (Hebrews 4, verse 14), or to have been made "higher than the heavens" (Hebrews 7, verse 26). But it would have to be said that there is some corporeal heaven outside and above the Heavens, and the same must be placed in a location, which sounder philosophy rejects. I now pass over in silence those who imagined 365 Heavens according to Irenaeus. I shall say at least something about the opinion of the adversaries of the Calvinist party: for they first fabricate some common Heaven in which Hercules, Palamedes, Numa Pompilius, or Scipio might live happily, according to that of Christ: "He who does not believe in the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him" (John 3, verses 18, 36). Secondly, they attribute to us a Ubiquistic Heaven.

### §. XV.

Indeed, whether GUSTAVUS inflicted a just punishment upon these disturbers could seem doubtful to someone. For writers testify with unanimous consent that they were seditious and looters of sacred things. It seemed better that they be removed from the midst than dismissed from the kingdom and sent away into other provinces. For most of the devil's ferments have such a nature that, even if you purge them from one region, they soon sprout up again more destructively in another. But the most religious GUSTAVUS is in no way to be reproached for the leniency of the punishment, since *hereticide* <note>original: "hæreticidium"</note> is repugnant to divine and human law alike, and supreme power over human minds is left to God alone. This dispute was once agitated between the Elector of Saxony and Philip, Landgrave of Hesse, regarding what punishment should be inflicted upon the Anabaptists. And finally, it was decided that for those who disapproved of the duties of the magistrates and incited sedition, capital punishment should be inflicted; that no one could with a clear conscience inflict the death penalty for an error in faith, but in the case of either rebellion or stubborn contumacy in propagating errors, where they either openly impugn the laws of the magistrate or hold assemblies against the so often issued and repeated edicts of princes. See Seckendorffius, *Luther. Book III, Sect. 13, §. XLII, p. 115-116.* GUSTAVUS could not deal otherwise with these superstitious men than with the papists, whose superstition, if not the same, was similar and deserved a similar punishment. He himself traveled through the provinces of the kingdom, visited the churches, inquired into the life and doctrine of the pastors, and did not wish to indulge in any vehemence of the priests or untimely rigor. for a little while, for thirty-three continuous days, he sailed content with only sky and water. The Spanish companions began first to murmur in secret, then soon to press with open insults, to think about killing him, finally, it was suggested that he be thrown into the sea: they claimed that they had been deceived by a man from Liguria, that they were being dragged into an abyss from which it would never be permitted to return. After the thirtieth day, driven by madness, they proclaimed that he should be led back, and they goaded the man not to proceed any further: he, however, by soft words and by ample hope, delaying day after day, soothed the angry men; he preached that they should be held accountable by the kings for treason if they plotted anything adverse against him, and if he refused to obey. At length, joyful, they receive the desired sight of land. With this first voyage he revealed only six islands, and of these, two of unheard-of magnitude: one of which he called Hispaniola, and the other Joanna; but he was not certain that Joanna was an island. As they were skirting the shores of some of them, they heard the nightingale singing among the dense forests in the month of November. He discovered huge rivers of fresh water and natural harbors capable of holding great fleets. Skirting the shores of Joanna, he traveled along the northern side from the west for no less than eight hundred miles (for they say one hundred and eighty leagues), thinking it to be a continent, because neither an end nor any sign of an end appeared on the island, as far as his eyes could discern: he decided to turn back; the swells of the sea also compelled him to return, for the shores of Joanna, through various bends, were turning and curving so much toward the north that northern winds were striking the ships more sharply, since winter was prevailing. Therefore, turning the prows to the east, he reports that he had found the island of Ophir: but when the charts of cosmographers are carefully considered, those are the islands of Antilia and others adjacent; he called this one Hispaniola: wishing to test the nature of the places on its northern side, he approached the land. When the hull of the larger ship struck a flat and blind rock covered by water, it was breached and remained stuck; the level surface of the hidden rock was a help to them, so they would not be submerged; therefore, with the rest, being doubtful, they led all the men out safely. There, having first landed on the earth, they saw indigenous people; who, seeing the unheard-of race arriving, gathered in a group and fled into the dense forests like timid hares from Gallic hounds. Our men pursued the multitude and captured only a woman; when they had led her to the ships, having satisfied her well with our food and wine, and having adorned her with clothes (for that entire nation of both sexes leads a life completely naked, content with nature), they left her free. When the woman had returned to her own people (for she knew where those fleeing were retreating) and had shown how wondrous was the attire and generosity of our men, all ran together to the shores in competition, thinking that the race had been sent from heaven. They brought gold, of which they had some abundance, to the ships by swimming; they traded gold for a piece of an earthenware dish or a glass cup. If our men shared a lace, or a bell, or a fragment of a mirror, or anything else, they exhibited as much gold as it pleased them to ask, or as much as each of them could obtain. When the matter had arrived at familiar commerce, and our men investigated the customs of the nations, they learned through signs and conjectures that that nation had kings. Descending from the ships, our men were honorably received by the king and the remaining natives; <margin>The admirable kindness of the people</margin> they rose to greet our men in all the ways they could and knew. With the sun tending toward the sunset, when our men knelt according to the Christian rite to give the sign of the angelic salutation <note>the Angelus</note>, they did the same. They also adored the cross in the way they had seen the Christians worship. From the ship which we said was dashed upon the rock, that nation brought our men and everything that was carried in it to the land in their own small boats, which they call canoes, so quickly and with such a happy spirit that no relatives among us, moved by greater compassion, could help their own. ### XXIX.

<margin>Proprie.</margin>
Verùm hoc in loco accipitur propriè: siquidem verbum *pará* generale est, ad cuiusque refructificationem pertinens. Vnde cum varijs coniungitur vocibus: quomodo in multis scripturæ dictis videre est.

### XXX.

<margin>Fructus ventris Davidis. Probatio. Ex testimonio Psalmi.</margin>
Hîc sufficit, ubi probaverimus, filium Dei unicum, & naturalem vocari, & esse fructum ventris Davidis: quomodò legimus Psalmo 132. 11. Iuravit Iehova ipsi David veritatem, non avertetur, sive deflectet, aut discedet, ab ea:

> De fructu ventris tui ponam super sedem, vel solium tuum.

### XXXI.

Quam promissionem etsi multi tantùm intelligunt de regno politico: tamen nos divum secuti Lutherum existimamus Deum iuramento confirmasse, ut de fructu ventris David ponatur rex; cuius regnum sit æternum.

### XXXII.

Ac sanè insignis hæc est promissio: quòd certam personam definit; nec finit successionem vagari in incerta persona.

### XXXIII.

Abraham, Isaac, Iacob, etiam habuerunt promissionem de Christo. Sed sub incerta persona: si respicias ad multiplicatam posteritatem.

### XXXIV.

In hac autem promissione est certa descriptio, quòd certa persona denominata est: ut, quamvis totus populus captivus esset abducendus; tamen, quamdiu posteritas Davidis superesset, spem regni retinerent.

### XXXV.

Fuit enim hæc familia, tanquam stella quædam in hoc

### XXXVI.

<margin>Ex concordantijs.</margin>
In Latinis Biblijs huic versui adduntur concordantiae: quae et ipsae ostendunt, Psalmistam hic loqui de Christo.

### XXXVII.

Tale est dictum illud 2. Samuelis 7. 12. Cum completi fuerint dies tui et dormieris cum patribus tuis, suscitabo semen tuum post te, quod egredietur de utero tuo: et firmabo regnum eius. Lucae 1. 55. Sicut locutus est ad patres nostros, Abraham, et semini eius in secula.

### XXXVIII.

In margine versionis Germanicae allegantur Psalmi 89. et 110. qui ex professo, quod facile demonstrari potest, loquuntur de Christo.

### XXXIX.

<margin>Ab authoritate orthodoxorum.</margin>
Simili modo hunc locum declarant Vrbanus Regius in Dialogo, Pomeranus, et alij fideles, atque orthodoxi interpretes.

### XL.

<margin>Fructus lumborum Davidis.</margin>
Huc absque omni dubitatione Petrus respicit Act. 2. 30. ubi Christum fructum Lumborum Davidis appellat, inquiens, Davidem, cum esset Propheta, scivisse: quod jurejurando jurasset illi Deus, de fructu Lumbi eius sedere super sedem eius.

### XLI.

<margin>Fructus terrae</margin>
Esaias capite 4. 2. eum nominat, ad afferendam eius veram humanitatem, fructum terrae: siquidem Gen. 3. 19. Homo terra est: quomodo septuaginta interpretantur:

<vocab>liberatio, Christus, captivitas Babylonica, Psalmi, Samuelis, Vrbanus Regius, Pomeranus, fructus lumborum Davidis, humanitas, septuaginta</vocab>

seed:
my only begotten son: who according to the flesh shall be your seed: which shall be generated from the flesh and blood of the most blessed virgin Mary: and shall come forth through a pure birth from the womb of the same virgin, by which he will trace his lineage from your family, and so forth.

-> XXV. <-

<margin>2. Because of the birth.</margin>
Then, because he was born from his lineage, Acts 13:23. From his seed, according to the promise, God brought forth to Israel a savior, Jesus. Romans 1:3. He promised the gospel concerning his son, who was born from the seed of David, according to the flesh.

-> XXVI. <-

<margin>3. Because of the authority of scripture. 4. Because of inheritance.</margin>
Furthermore, this reason also may be brought forward: because he is so frequently called this in the Prophets, and in the common speech of the people. Finally, because he is the heir of the promises of David, and his successor in the kingdom of Israel.

-> XXVII. <-

<margin>Why David is named first.</margin>
Moreover, as Erasmus notes, he names David first, not only because the series of the genealogy might be woven more conveniently and without repetition, which is the reason provided by the divine Jerome: but also because his memory was both more recent and more celebrated among the Hebrews, which is the reason provided by Chrysostom.

-> XXVIII. <-

<margin>Fruit. Metaphorical meaning.</margin>
Now we will arrive at the term fruit: which, as Mercerus indicates from Forsterus, whom he often imitates, is sometimes used figuratively or metaphorically for a reward, just as the Greek <term>karpos</term> <gloss>fruit</gloss> is akin to the Hebrew <term>peri</term> <gloss>fruit</gloss>, as in Psalm 58:12. And a man shall say, having seen such destruction of the wicked and the preservation of the pious, certainly there is a fruit for the righteous, that is, the righteous and pious finally receive the fruit of their piety: even if at first glance the opposite may appear. Proverbs 31:16. With the fruit of her hands she planted a vineyard. Ibid, verse 31. Give her of the fruit of her hands.

<margin>3. Ob authoritatem scripturae. 4. Haereditatis causa.</margin>
Tùm etiam haec causa afferri potest: quia sic crebrò vocatur in Prophetis, et communi sermone populi. Denique, quia promissionum Davidis haeres, et eius in regno Israelis successor est.

-> XXVII. <-

<margin>Cur David prius nominetur.</margin>
Davidem porrò, ut annotat Erasmus, priorem nominat, non solùm ob id, quòd commodiùs, citráque repetitionem genealogiae series texeretur, quam causam reddidit divus Hieronymus: verùm etiam quòd huius esset apud Hebraeos et recentior et celebrior memoria, quod affert Chrysostomus.

-> XXVIII. <-

<margin>Fructus. Metaphorica significatio.</margin>
Nunc perveniemus ad vocabulum fructus: quod ut indicat Mercerus ex Forstero, quem saepè imitatur, aliquando figuratè vel metaphoricè, pro mercede usurpatur, sicut Graecis κάρπος, Hebraeo *peri* vicinum, ut Psalmo 58. 12. Et dicet homo, visa tali internecione impiorum, et conservatione piorum, utique est fructus iusto, hoc est, iusti, et pii tandem fructum percipiunt suae pietatis: etiam si prima fronte contrarium appareat. Proverb. 31. 16. de fructu manuum suarum plantavit vineam. Ibidem vers. 31. Date ei de fructu manuum suarum.

### XLII.

Verba formalia, desumpta ex textu Hebræo, sunt: In die illa erit &c. fructus terræ in sublimitate & in decore evasioni Israel, hoc est eo tempore, quo abijcietur gens Iudaica, Christus erit gratus, amabilis & acceptus atque etiam in summa dignitate & honore maximo apud eos Israelitas, qui in Christum credunt, & sic damnationem effugiunt.

### XLIII.

<margin>
Fructus benedictus ventris Mariæ.
</margin>
Hic statim subijciemus: quod Lucæ 1.42. ab Elizabetha vocatur fructus benedictus ventris Mariæ benedictæ.

### XLIIII.

Elizabetha, cognata Mariæ, repleta fuit Spiritu Sancto, ut Evangelista hic dicit, versu 41. Etenim in sexum quoque muliebrem Spiritus Sanctus sua dona conferre solet: quæ res hunc sexum à contemptu vindicare debet.

### XLV.

Ideò præ ingenti gaudio, haud ignara conceptionis Mariæ, & Messiæ exclamavit voce magna: atque miraculosum, & omni memoria inauditum hoc Dei opus honorificè prædicavit, usa illis verbis, quorum anteà mentio facta est.

### XLVI.

<margin>
Fructus dicitur 1. respectu promissionum & expectationis Patrum.
</margin>
Fructus dicitur Christus (quod non reticendum puto,) Primùm propter manifestationem: dum hactenus in spe promissionum latuit, nunc autem ad finem perventum est & usus promissionum tandem percipitur Sic igitur fructus est, respectu promissionum, & expectationis Patrum.

### §. XXIII.

It is beyond controversy that this privilege is inviolable in the place of the markets; but whether the same thing is sacred in the approach and return, or in the places through which market-goers both approach and depart, is not undeservedly doubted. For it seems that it was given for a certain place, and thus, being bound to it, cannot be extended to other places. But the rightly praised Sichard maintains the affirmative here, because he who cannot safely approach and depart does not come quietly or securely. Whence the Emperor Maximilian I, with the privilege of the markets granted to the Leipzigers, as referenced by Carpzovius in the aforementioned chapter 30, definition 28, inserted these words: Likewise the goods and properties which are driven and led to and from designated markets and storehouses shall not be stopped, hindered, or legally arrested, etc. It is required, however, that the approach and departure take place on the days of the markets, and through those places which are under the empire of the Prince granting the solemn markets; otherwise, as I would establish as undoubtedly true with the praised Carpzovius in the aforementioned definition 28, merchants in the places through which they pass either before or after the markets can not only be summoned, but their persons and things can also be detained by arrest, because the market privilege ceases when the markets have not yet begun or have already finished. And if before the markets or when they are finished it is permitted for a Creditor to summon and arrest his Debtor in the very place of the markets, how much more will it be permitted for him in the places through which the debtor prepares his approach or return?

Unde Imperator *Maximilianus I.* privilegio nundinali *Lipsiensibus* concesso referente *Carpzovio dicto capite 30. definitione 28.* haec inseruit verba: Desgleichen die Wahren und Güter/ so zu und von bestimmten Märckten und Niederlagen getrieben und geführet werden/ nicht sollen auffgehalten/ verhindert/ oder rechtlichen arrestiret werden/ etc. Requiritur tamen, ut accessus et recessus fiat diebus nundinarum, perque illa loca, quae sub imperio sunt Principis nundinas solennes indulgentis; alias cum laudatum *Carpzovio dicto definitione 28.* indubius statuerem, mercatores in locis per quos vel ante vel post nundinas transeunt, non tantùm conveniri, sed et personas resque eorum arresto detineri posse, quia nundinis nondum coeptis, vel jam finitis privilegium nundinale cessat. It was not the feeling of my mind that the Son of God had ever admitted any wickedness into Himself and in His own person. Far be that impiety. Truly, I only wished to indicate with those words that Christ had voluntarily taken upon Himself the burden of making atonement for all sins that were committed by other men. Let whoever wishes read my book. Certainly, he will extract nothing else from it than what I have just said. **CALV.** However your mind may have been, the words certainly smell no less of blasphemous horror than mine do. **AEAC.** Be silent. That is enough words. Let us finally come to our business. You have heard, judges, what the case of these men is. Now, therefore, it is incumbent upon you, by virtue of your office, that each one of you deliver his own sentence. What do you think, Minos? **LUTH.** We ask for grace. **CALV.** We implore mercy, judges. **AEAC.** There is no grace among the dead, no pity in Orcus <note>the Underworld</note>. Justice alone holds the kingdom here and commands. Therefore, unless you wish to be punished worse, take care to mutter nothing from now on. Tell me, Minos, what is your opinion, or by what punishment do you think these culprits should be afflicted? **MIN.** If, indeed, there were in Hell some stable of Augeas, or a pigsty, I would clearly sentence this foul pair of shades to be tormented there forever in swine dung and filth. The squalid life of both clearly deserves this. But now, since we have no pigsty here in Orcus, I will consider it better to send them to the lair of the three-throated Cerberus, on the condition and omen that Luther should lie back at the dung-gate of Cerberus, to be fed only on the farts, dung, and urine of the Acherontic dog. I judge it clearly fair that he, who in life had these things so familiar and frequent in his mouth and pen, should have them constant when dead. Calvin, however, should always be awake and sleepless in the front part of the cave, and, tormented by rabies, hunger, and thirst, together with Cerberus, should bark and snarl day and night at Mercury, and Charon, and all the gods, and even the ghosts of men who sail across here to us; and with rabid clamor, just as he acted in life, so let him also infest them when dead. Error in hoc latet, quod perperam de constitutione imaginis Dei quacunque accipitur perfectio, quippe quae competat essentiae Dei; in quo inest insignis confusio. At vero si imago Dei non nisi perfecta apprehenditur, absolute posita, quia perfectus Deus est, certe nec de Adamo nondum lapso dici illa potuerit, quoniam similiter propter mentionem Dei, qui infinitus est, conceperis forte infinitam. Qua quidem instantia quid clarius? Nec quidquam incommodi habet, si renatis tribuatur imago Dei eadem, quae homini concreata, atque ab Adamo deperdita est. Quod si aequalis praedicaretur, fieret non sine errore: ast eandem esse, nihil designat, nisi imaginis Dei unam eandemque veritatem. Neque enim qui audit, regenitos recepisse imaginem Dei, quam Adamus perdidit, eo ipso de perfectione cogitat, quod ea perfecta fuerit, sed de eo, quid per imaginem Dei intelligendum sit; tantumque abest, ut hujusmodi locutio perfectionem una insinuet, ut potius penes audientem nova quaestione fuerit opus, an, qui ipsam recuperent, possideant perfectam? § XXIX. An autem uterqve parens, vel solus tantum pater, hunc filium rebellem adducere ad synedrium debuerit disputatur. *Theodoretus Tomus 1. operum editione Parisiis pagina 168.* existimat, & Patrem & Matrem consentire in accusatione filii hujus debuisse, anteqvam potuerit occidi. Qvæ sententia albo approbatur calculo in *Mischna de synedriis capite 8. citato § 4.* ubi dicitur: *si pater ejus velit (accusare illum) mater autem nolit, vel si pater noluerit, mater autem velit, non fit filius rebellis & contumax donec ambo voluerint.* Deinde subjungitur: *Si unus illorum (parentum) sit mutilus, vel claudus, vel mutus, vel cæcus, vel surdus, non fit filius rebellis & contumax: qvia dicitur: & prehendent illum pater & mater ejus: ergo non debent esse mutili, & educent illum, ergo non debent esse claudi, & dicent, ergo non debent esse muti, hic noster filius, ergo non debent esse cæci, non audit vocem nostram ergo non debent esse surdi.*

§ XXX. Sed nova oritur Quæstio: an Deuteronomii 21. versus 22. & 23. *Cum autem fuerit in viro peccatum qvod mereatur mortem, & occidatur, & suspendas illum in ligno, non pernoctabit cadaver ejus in ligno, sed sepeliendo sepelies illum eo die, qvoniam maledictus Dei est suspensus, & non immundabis terram tuam, qvam Jehova Deus tuus dat tibi in possessionem*, an inquam illi versus referri ad filium rebellem & contumacem debeant? Sane veteres Hebræi in ea sunt sententia, & dicunt, si parentes filio parcant, illumqve accusare nolint, qvod tum occidatur a synedrio, sive obruatur lapidibus, suspendaturqve, qvia si notorius peccator est, inquiritur in illum a senatu. *Vid. jarchii in hoc loco & Elias Misrachi, diligentissimus jarchii interpres, in hoc loco editione Cracoviensi folio 304. columna 4.*

§ XXXI. Restat ut de pernoctatione in ligno aliqva adjiciamus. Hoc certum est, suspendio post mortem fuisse punitos reos apud veteres Hebræos, ut inter alios testatur *Obadias de Saphorno in Biur al Hattora editione Venetiis folio 73. columna 1.*, ubi suspendium

Venet. fol. 93. col. 1. inf.* Poenam enim fuisse suspensionem patet, ut docet *Calovius* in *Deut. 21.* Cur autem non debuerint relinqui cadavera in ligno, inquirendum est.

§. XXXII. *Jacobus Bolducius Tom. 2. in librum job. edit. Paris. p. 132.* ex *Andrea Masio* refert rationem, cur lex supplicio crucis affectos sepeliri voluerit, esse hanc, quoniam ex diutino in cruce spectaculo facile deduci quis in extinctae animae opinionem posse videretur, minusque recte de futura corporum resurrectione cogitare.

§. XXXIII. Sed potior videtur fuisse ratio, ne tactu cadaveris immundarentur homines, inprimis cum immundities ex mortuo contracta in gente Hebraea inter omnes immundities esset maxima. Quo tendit expositio *Lucae Osiandri in Deut. 21. in fin.*

§. XXXIV. Atque sic suspendium excussum est, quomodo se apud judaeos habuerit. Licet autem lignum in quo rei suspendebantur, vocari possit patibulum, ut illud vocat *Jeckutbiel* in versione bibliorum Germanica in *Deut. 21. edit. Amstelod.* & lignum quoque sumatur pro patibulo docente *Flacio*, in *clave tit. lignum, edit. Jenensis p. 587.* tamen supplicium crucifixionis apud Hebraeos usitatum non fuit, quia non inter supplicia crucifixio tanquam peculiare supplicium recensetur, sed tantum suspensionis, tanquam alterius supplicii consequentis, mentio injicitur. Nec verbum תלה praecise significat suspendere vivum hominem, vel in crucem agere, cum etiam de illis rebus usurpetur, in quas crucifixio non cadit; v. g. suspendi dicuntur in clavo ligneo carnes vel pisces, vel panes, quae non dicuntur crucifigi. XXVII. *Moses Nachmanides of Gerona* also admits, in *Biur al Hattora, Venice edition, printed without the Biblical text, fol. 146, col. 2*, that this rebellious son not only despised his Parents and opposed them, but was also a glutton and a drunkard, who shamelessly transgressed the Law of God, which mandates holiness, and that he had been afflicted with the penalty of Stoning, so that others might take an example from it and revere the divine law.

§. XXVIII. Hence also *Bechaj* writes in *Biur al Hattora, Cracow edition, fol. 127, col. 3*, that this rebellious son transgressed the divine precepts, and hence had to be led by his parents to the Sanhedrin, so that it might be shown that parents must love God and His precepts more than their son, although the love of parents for their children is most strong.

about which it is concerned, insofar as reason or sense determines that this is good for oneself, for one's own, or for the whole society, according to the reason of this triple good which the will desires, there is also a triple distinction of Ethics. For Ethics, specifically so-called, governs the will privately so that it may desire what is good for itself, lest it commit anything unworthy of itself or little decent, and it hands down virtues common to all men. Economics governs the will so that it may desire what is good for one's own, and it hands down the method of increasing household affairs. Politics, however, governs the will so that it may desire what is advantageous to the whole society, lest harm be brought upon the community, and it hands down the virtues proper to those who administer the republic. I use here the term good generally for the honest, useful, and pleasant good.

In Civil Law, however, to lesser Magistrates who by no means can restore against the sentence of superiors (Law 18, beginning, Digest on Minors). By the same law, only the Prince restores against the sentence of the Prince, and indeed rarely and only on account of new allegations (said Law 18, section 1). Similarly, only the Prince restores against a sentence spoken by the Procurator of Caesar or the *rationalis* (Law 1, Code on where and before whom), or spoken by another in his stead (*vice sacra*) (Law 3, Code if against a decided matter; said Law 18, section 'the same', on minors), or spoken by him whom the Prince himself gave as judge (said law 'a minor however', section 'but even if', Digest on Minors).

So far Reinerius, whose testimony has the greater weight with me and is of more value because he was an Inquisitor throughout Lombardy, or a censor of those who were held as heretics among the Romanists.

(p) This book of Reinerius against the Waldensians exists not only in the second part of the fourth Tome of the *Library of the Fathers*, fourth edition, with the Prolegomena of the Jesuit Jacob Gretser, as testified by Forbes in book 7, chapter 15, § 1, folio 371. He flourished in the year 1254, as attested by Antonius Senensis, in the aforementioned Prolegomena of Gretser, ch. 9; see Forbes, l. c., § 2, f. 372. He was a monk of the Order of Preachers; he was Italian by nationality, as is the author Spanheim, page 521 and 524; see *Gotha History* in the cited place.

Wherefore, since because of the multitude of sins and the impenitent heart of many we see the censure of divine vengeance threatening the people—which, as the pestilence wanders far and wide, rages more cruelly against miserable and heedless souls, which also perishes entirely in the body itself—while amidst the scourges by which the heavenly Father strives to call us back to himself, not only is there no running to the lamentations of penance, but it is sinned more freely and even obstinately; while charity cools among Kings and Princes who dissent among themselves to the peril of their subjects; it has seemed good to us in these calamities and dangers, adhering to the footsteps of the holy fathers and also of our predecessors, to apply the office of apostolic exhortation, so that we may appease with weeping and penance the God whom we have provoked to anger by sinning through dissensions and wars, which are waged against Christ’s faithful when they ought to be waged against the enemies of Christ’s name. Wherefore, we warn and exhort in the Lord all Christ’s faithful of either sex, as well religious as secular, of whatever status, dignity, and preeminence, as well of our beloved city as of any other cities and dioceses, residing both in Italy and outside Italy, in virtue of holy obedience, that from the second feria <note>Monday</note> after the publication of these presents made in the City and other cities and dioceses, everyone should strive to examine their conscience with diligent inquiry and endeavor to prepare for the purest confession of all their sins, which they will be able to fulfill within the space of three days. Then, on the fourth feria <note>Wednesday</note>, the sixth feria <note>Friday</note>, and the sabbath <note>Saturday</note> of that week in which the publication itself shall have been made in the aforementioned cities and dioceses, all those constituted at a legitimate age should fast, unless they are held by a just impediment, meanwhile all alike applying themselves to assiduous and devout prayers, so that we may be able to receive the remedies of divine mercy more quickly to extinguish wars, pestilence, and other such evils, and to obtain peace. Figuram.xvi. laterum (ut diximus) ita constituas / ut e singulis.xxxii. partibus et minutis sex xxx. unum latus efficiat: qui videlicet numerus quater ductus / quarta celi parte implet hoc est partes.xc. que ratio docet gradus duos et sex cum dimidiato gradu sexdecies multiplicatos / trecentos et sexaginta gradus complere: quot gradus totus celi ambitus est. Renowned in pedigree, fame, wealth, beauty, and the piety of her parents, and in every womanly grace; the maiden whom Venus sprinkled with Idalian juices and much nectar, and joyfully added the grace of beauty, approved morals, and every honor of talent, to whom (if the lying Phoebus has not struck my heart with a vain omen) after thrice three months, Lucina <note>goddess of childbirth</note> will bring the light of birth, nearby. But lest what I, the seer, augur should vanish, may the Aeneian mother <note>Venus</note> preside over your bed.

These things for you, O GENEROUS HERO, while the hoped-for day brings the marriage torches, while your wife is led to you—royal offspring, famous, beautiful, chaste, neither rude in talent nor lacking true endowment—GENTIUS, having experienced you recently as a friend to the Muses and honoring you because of the Muses and eloquent tongues with the affection of a rejoicing mind, and wishing that love, with head veiled in laurel, might surround the bed and sustain the living fire in your hearts, and make it grow daily as much as the fresh shoots of the pine grow in the new spring. I stop: the dishes on the tables are steaming with feasts, and they leave the stomach barking with hunger near the words.

But the adversary turns to other matters and seeks a comparison in many things without any foundation. If it pleases him to act in this way, let us continue to draw conclusions with the same rashness and falsehood: As Jonah was in the whale with his body; so Christ was in hell (which the Roman Catholics <note>original: "Pontificii"</note> desire) with his body. As Jonah did not deliver anyone from the fish; so Christ delivered no one from hell. As Jonah was swallowed by the fish alive and clothed; so Christ was admitted into hell while still alive and in his clothes.

### IV.

Thirdly, the defender of Roman superstition brings <term>Hieronymus</term> <gloss>Jerome</gloss> into the battle line, commenting on chapter 2 of Jonah with these words: *as the heart is in the middle of a living creature, so hell is said to be in the middle of the earth.* He also praises <term>Irenaeus</term>, <term>Tertullianus</term> <gloss>Tertullian</gloss>, and <term>Nyssenus</term> <gloss>Gregory of Nyssa</gloss>, who move in this direction. But we have already warned that no protection should be sought in them, since they define and assert things that are uncertain and unknown to the Holy Scriptures. Even if we were to grant that Christ broke through to the center of the Earth; it would still burden the Roman Catholics to prove as absolute certainty that Hell is found there with those appendages, before any conclusion whatsoever can be reached about the Savior's descent according to their view. Moreover, we oppose battle line with battle line: namely, <term>Chrysostomus</term> <gloss>John Chrysostom</gloss> in Homily 44 on Matthew, and <term>Bernhardus</term> <gloss>Bernard of Clairvaux</gloss> in Sermon 1 on the Death of the Monk Humbert, who fight for our side.

### V.

As for what others say, that Christ’s tomb was not in the *Earth*, and therefore not in the *Heart of the Earth*, but in a *Rock*; this is solved by laughter rather than by reason. For who would remove rocks from the Terrestrial Globe, and say that this solid and compact earth is not earth.

From what has been said, it appears that the third chapter, paragraph 3 of Monzambanus on the state of the German Empire was propelled by envy rather than by a study of truth, as he pronounces judgment below: That by such pacts, the power of the Emperor, which he obtains over the dominions of the Princes as Lord of the fief, is entirely evaded.

**XLVI.** Furthermore, the nature of the Confraternity bids one to explore the consent of the previous Confratres <gloss>fellow brothers</gloss>, if any exist, lest their right, which they have acquired in a certain hope of succession, be subverted without their knowledge and against their will, as Master Bechmann correctly warns in his *Discourse*, chapter 3, folio 1, paragraph 1.

**XLVII.** Finally, it will be advisable not to omit the consent of the subjects, *the gathered Land-Estates*, especially if a powerful province is in question, whose inhabitants, having taken up arms, are able to defend themselves against a lord unknown to them and intruded upon them against their will. Compare the Renewal of the Saxon-Hessian Confraternity of the year 1555 in Limnaeus, *Public Law* 4, 8, 162, folio 206, and Bechmann in the said place.

**XLIIX.** So much for the natural elements after the manner of the institution: let us touch upon the accidental elements of the Confraternity, that is, those which can be absent while the substance and nature of the thing are saved, and yet cannot be present unless the thing subsists. To this is referred, first, the solemnity of the Oath, which is performed either by the Confratres themselves to one another, or by their subjects to them, and is called the Homage of subjection, *Land-homage or hereditary duty*: concerning which compare George Ritter's elegant treatise. Waremundus of Ehrenberg in his *Meditation on Leagues*, book 2, chapter 1, number 122 and following, thinks it safer that the former be performed bodily by the Confratres themselves due to the importance of the business. And that oath is rightly for the most part rejected after the confirmation of the Lord of the Fief, lest a particle of divine air be injured by an oath conceived in vain.

Thence Ladislas, his brother, takes possession of the empire, whom Roman Pontiffs later admitted into the number of the Saints, distinguished for his piety. bearing witness), it is not of the Macrocosm suffering under the vanity of the flesh (Romans VIII. 21), but flourishing and glorying in the truth of God the Creator, it is not of grace, but of nature, it is not done through the word and sacrament, but through the intent of the creative sanctification, it is not of the Gospel, but of the law, it is not of the Spirit of recreation, but of creation, not of spiritual reformation, but of natural formation, not of spiritual regeneration, but of causal generation, not of gracious renovation, but of the first fabrication, etc. For all creatures were then flourishing in their first bloom, and had not yet lost the co-created bloom through the most miserable fall of man, and thus they always contended in a certain most beautiful harmony toward this sanctification of the Creator.

12. (III) *The Exodus of Sanctification*, because it is certain that the whole sanctification of the *seventh day*, or even of all creatures on the seventh day, looked finally not so much to the remaining creatures as to the scope of all the remaining creatures, the *Microcosm* itself, *Man*. For just as through the *First Elohim* the Creator things were Said, and made, or created, and truly through the *Blessing Elohim*, or the *Orator and Dispenser of the Creative Blessing*, all things were adorned with various blessings for the sake of man, or for his use and fruit: so also through the *sanctifying Third Elohim* they were destined for no other end than for the sake of man, for sanctification, or the glorification of the divine Name. *Jehovah Elohim* himself is the best interpreter of his own words, and indeed not only elsewhere in the sacred scriptures, but most especially in the august promulgation of the Decalogue, he sufficiently explains this, just as we recited the express words from *Exodus XX. 9* and following in paragraph 9, in which place all this sanctification is solemnly accommodated to Man in clear words. And furthermore the *Psalmist* opens this secret to us here and there, and shows the divine artifices of the present sanctification by various examples, that surely men ought to excite the creatures to the praise, glorification, and sanctification of the Divine Name, and at the same time ought to search out divine praises more studiously in the creatures, and conveniently use all things likewise that are in the creatures for the sanctification, celebration, and glorification of the Name, which we could certainly demonstrate to the eye with many *Psalms*, if we wished now to add more to the preceding points.

<summary>This text distinguishes between the initial creative sanctification by Jehovah and the later redemptive work of the Messiah. It highlights that the original sanctification, involving the entire Macrocosm and the Microcosm of man, was a natural and causal order, which the Psalmist urges humans to continue through the celebration of God's name in creation.</summary>

A gloss and Johannes Campegius, cited by Nicolaus Intrighiolus, a professor in Catania, Sicily, call it anomalous. Oldendorpius, Duarenus, and Lord Struvius, who also praises Jason for this opinion, write that it is simply of good faith. Baldus, Bertachinus, Petrus Nicolaus Mozzius, and Zasius concede this only in the case where it has been initiated with a Prince. But it is of strict law according to Alvarotto, Matthaeus de Afflictis, Caccialupo, Hanneton, Curtius Junior, Clarus, Schraderus, Rosenthal, Intrighiolus, Arumaeus, and Setserus. To us, the arguments of Lord Ludwell—who departs here from the common opinion and does not acknowledge any feudal contract distinct from other contracts and businesses—do not seem entirely dismissible.

## V.

Lord Ludwell, Vulteius, Gothofredus Antonius, Borcholt, Gaeddaeus, Schneidwin, Contius, Wilhelmus Fornerius, Sonsbecius, and Niellius refer succession to the modes of acquiring a Feud. Lord Carpzovius, Suevius, Hunnius, Rittershusius, Finckelthusius, and Sculzius deny this, wishing it to pertain to the modes of constituting. Lord Struvius thinks it is a mode of neither constituting nor acquiring, as he refers those only to a new Feud. We shall defend the opinion of the former, which we are persuaded also accords with the reason of the law.

## VI.

Schraderus and Gyphanius write that a Feud is constituted by prescription. Less correctly. For prescription does not claim a place among the modes of constituting, but rather of acquiring a Feud, as Lord Ludwell and Lord Snobelius rightly warn after Vulteius and others.

### LVI.

Food and drink should be moderate; food should incline toward dryness, be of good juice, easy to digest, pure, simple, and sparse; it should not be taken unless the stomach is urgent and the previous residues have been excreted. Dinner should be more frugal than lunch. Roasted things are more beneficial than boiled ones, and they should not be seasoned too much. Drink should be medicated, or thin, well-purified beer, or water for those who are thinner. It must be highly avoided if made colder by ice or saltpeter. One should not drink unless some solid food has been ingested. Not all use of wine is to be proscribed, however, for in those whose stomach is weakened, whose natural heat is dissolved, in delicate natures whose body is enervated, and in those with an excess of cold humors, the drinking of wine is necessary. Reddish, well-purified, pure, not very watery, not sulfurous, and not containing much tartar or earthy salt wines are praised; one must abstain entirely from sweet wine. Rhenish, Rhaetian, and <term>Nicrina</term> <gloss>wines from the Necker region</gloss> are praised, as are clear and year-old wines; wine of absinthe, sage wine, wine of blessed thistle, and of betony.

### LVII.

In sleep and vigils, moderation should also be maintained; although vigils dry the body, they also inflame it; midday sleep is to be avoided. If one has spent a sleepless night, one may sleep a little at midday, not immediately after food, but at least after an hour; nor should one sleep immediately after dinner, even if it is frugal. Movement should also be moderate; exercises are beneficial, but not violent, nor should one ride on horseback. Exercises should be carried out until the beginning of sweat, and they should precede food, and be performed at least twice a week. Affects of the mind, especially anger and sadness, must be restrained by the bridle of prudence, for they easily lead from a natural to a preternatural state. Galen, Book 3 of the *Art of Medicine*, text 16. Venus should be most moderate.

### LVIII.

The bowels should also perform their duty daily; if not, they must be aided by art, by means of raisins without seeds, or by dishes made from beet, spinach, cabbage, oil, and salt. Butter with sugar is the medicine of the elderly for softening the bowels. Take the root of parsley, cook it well, add fresh butter and sugar; let a draught of this broth be taken before lunch.

### §. XIII.

And indeed, as far as temples are concerned, they were generally erected in honor of Kings and Princes, as they were the ones given a greater opportunity to promote public safety. It is said that the Babylonians first built a temple to the monarch Belus, and treated him with divine honors before the gods, which temple PLINY, lib. VI, H.N., cap. 26, reports to have lasted in his own time. See PAUSANIAS in *Attica*, GYRALDUS, *Syntagma II, HISTORY OF THE GODS*, p. 180, see CHRISTOPH MATTHIAE in *Historical Theater*, p. 22. Thus, Dio records that temples were founded at Nicaea for Gaius Julius Caesar, the first of the Roman Monarchs, and also for Augustus, the successor of Julius, at Pergamon. Josephus likewise handed down to memory that a temple was built for that same Augustus by Herod. For, having received a large part of his kingdom from Augustus, Herod built a magnificent temple in honor of his benefactor <note>original: "Evergetae"</note> at the springs of the Jordan. See CALVISIUS, *CHRONOLOGICAL WORK*, p. 281, 285.

### §. XIV.

But it is clear from histories that temples were erected not only to Kings and Princes, but also to others (though by Christians, not heathens, and for a different end and manner). For those temples were built for Julius Caesar and Octavian Augustus so that they could be treated with divine worship, just as it was nothing new for the Gentiles to refer Kings or Queens into the number of the Gods. See BERNEGG, JUSTIN, lib. XIV, c. 1, & lib. XVIII, c. 6. But those temples about which we are speaking here (for we are speaking of those which have been dedicated and preserved by Christians to certain individuals; otherwise, it is known from Trogus that after the death of Pythagoras, a temple was made from his house and he was worshiped as a God) were constructed primarily in honor and glory of God, as their authors profess, and then in recollection and memory of certain pious and good men. This is evident from temples built and dedicated to Martyrs. See Calvisius, l.c., p. 479, 484.

->## SIXTH ASSERTION.<-

The form of a coin is seen in the public value, which distinguishes currency from metal and raw mass. Value, understood generally, encompasses three essential requirements: Weight, Character, and Assessment, which carry before them the goodness of the material, the truth of the weight, and the justice of the assessment. The weight of a coin forged from gold or silver must be certain and legitimate, and thus as much in the coin as in the raw mass, having deducted the costs of labor *a*. The character must express the image or insignia of the Prince and of him who by concession or privilege mints coins, so that the Insignia of Majesty and the Prince may be a witness of truth and justice in the currency *b*. The assessment is the price or public and fair estimation of a coin, not exceeding the goodness of the material and the quantity of the weight, lest otherwise the Prince offend the law of nations, to whom the coin belongs, and the communion of commerce *c*. Adjuncts of this form are the size of the coin, the round figure, the number of the value, the year, and the name of the currency *d*.

*a* For a coin, whatever it is, is entirely so by the benefit of the form impressed by public authority, by argument of the law <note>Julian, Digest on exhibiting, law 1. Digest on contracting a purchase.</note> For the form causes it to be called a coin, which was gold and silver, <note>law "who false" 19, verb "to form", Digest on the Cornelian Law on forgeries; law "elegantly" § "who rejects", Digest on the pledge action.</note> Weight, established by public faith and legitimately, excludes all fraud and imposture, and instructs the ignorant commoners regarding the truth, so that there was no need for the faith of a scale, to which we have today relapsed, <note>by argument of law 1, Digest on contracting a purchase, chapter "how much", extra on oaths; Coler. 4. on executive process, chapter 10, number 7. Duarenus 1. of disputes 6. add law 1 & 3, Code on the power of old coinage. Weight is written for gold coins and Thalers in the Monetary Ordinance of 1559. § "Ferner die gülden Müng." Imperial Recess of 1566. §.</note>

<note>Decorative red drop cap Q</note>Why have the nations raged: * & the people meditated on empty things?
The kings of the earth stood up, & the princes met together: * against the Lord, & against his Christ.
Let us break their bonds: * & let us cast away their yoke from us.
He who dwells in heaven, will laugh at them: * & the Lord will mock them.
Then he will speak to them in his anger: * & will trouble them in his fury.
But I am appointed king by him over Sion his holy mount: * preaching his commandment.
The Lord said to me: * you are my son, this day I have begotten you.
Ask of me, & I will give you the nations as your inheritance: * & the ends of the earth as your possession.
You will rule them with a rod of iron: * & you will shatter them like a potter's vessel.
And now O kings understand: * receive instruction you who judge the earth.
Serve the Lord with fear: * & exult to him with trembling.
Apprehend discipline, lest at some time the Lord be angry: * & you perish from the just way.
When his anger has enkindled in a short time: * blessed are all who trust in him.

<column-break/>

Psalm 6.
<note>Decorative red drop cap D</note>O Lord, do not argue with me in your fury: * nor in your anger chastise me.
Have mercy on me O Lord, for I am weak: * heal me O Lord, for my bones are troubled.
And my soul is troubled exceedingly: * but you O Lord how long?
Turn O Lord, & rescue my soul: * save me for the sake of your mercy.
For there is no one in death who is mindful of you: * moreover in hell who will confess to you?
I have labored in my groaning, I will wash my bed every night: * I will water my couch with my tears.
My eye is troubled by fury: * I have grown old among all my enemies.
Depart from me all you who work iniquity: * for the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping.
The Lord has heard my supplication: * the Lord has received my prayer.
May all my enemies be ashamed & troubled exceedingly: * may they be turned back & be ashamed very quickly.

— V —

Phantasie allein vergegenwärtigt sich die einzelnen Akte des Dramas, welches sich in der Seele der Volksmassen abspielte, als sie zwischen Ormuzd und der Trinität hin- und herschwankten. Wir kennen nur das Ergebnis des Kampfes: der Mithriacismus wurde besiegt, und zweifellos mußte er es werden. Jedoch ist seine Niederlage nicht ausschließlich der Überlegenheit der evangelischen Moral oder der apostolischen Predigt gegenüber der Lehre der Mysterien zuzuschreiben; er ist nicht lediglich deshalb zu Grunde gegangen, weil er von der ererbten Last einer überlebten Vergangenheit zu Boden gedrückt wurde, sondern auch, weil seine Liturgie und seine Theologie zu asiatisch geblieben war, als daß der römische Geist sie ohne Widerstreben hätte acceptieren können. Umgekehrt blieb ebenderselbe Kampf, der zu gleicher Zeit in Irân zwischen den beiden Rivalen entbrannt war, für die Christen ohne Erfolg, wonicht ohne Ehre, und in den Staaten der Sassaniden ließ sich der Zoroastrismus niemals ernstlich antasten.

Aber die Niederlage Mithras bedeutete nicht das Ende seiner Macht. Er hatte die Geister für die Aufnahme eines neuen Glaubens vorbereitet, der — wie er selbst — von den Ufern des Euphrat kam und mit veränderter Taktik die Feindseligkeiten wieder eröffnete. Der Manichäismus erschien als sein Erbe und setzte sein Werk fort. Es war der letzte Ansturm, den Persien auf den Occident unternahm, und er war blutiger als die anderen — aber auch er sollte schließlich an der Widerstandsfähigkeit des christlichen Reiches scheitern.

Diese flüchtige Skizze wird, wie ich hoffe, die Wichtigkeit der Geschichte des Mithriacismus erkennen lassen. Ein Seitenschößling des alten mazdäischen Stammes, hat er in vieler Beziehung die Eigentümlichkeiten der alten Naturreligion der iranischen Stämme bewahrt und läßt uns vergleichsweise die so umstrittene Tragweite der avestischen Reformation besser verstehen. Anderseits hat er gewisse Lehren der Kirche wenn nicht inspiriert, so doch wenigstens

— VI —

präzisieren geholfen, wie die Vorstellungen von den höllischen Mächten und vom Ende der Welt. So trägt sein Aufkommen wie sein Untergang dazu bei, die Entstehungsgeschichte zweier großer Religionen aufzuhellen. In der Zeit seiner Vollkraft übte er einen nicht minder bemerkenswerten Einfluß auf die römische Gesellschaft und die römische Regierung aus. Vielleicht war Europa niemals, selbst nicht in der Epoche der mohammedanischen Invasionen, näher daran asiatisch zu werden als im 3. Jahrhundert unserer Ära; und es gab eine Zeit, in welcher der Cäsarismus anscheinend im Begriffe stand, sich in ein Khalifat zu verwandeln. Man hat oft auf die Ähnlichkeit hingewiesen, welche zwischen dem Hofe Diokletians und dem der Chosroës besteht. Der Sonnenkult und namentlich die mazdäischen Theorien machten die Ideen populär, auf welche die vergötterten Herrscher ihren monarchischen Absolutismus zu gründen suchten. Die rapide Ausbreitung der persischen Mysterien in allen Klassen der Bevölkerung diente in bewunderungswürdiger Weise dem politischen Ehrgeiz der Kaiser. Eine Sturmflut von iranischen und semitischen Gedanken brach herein, welche fast alles verschlang, was der griechische oder römische Geist in mühevoller Arbeit aufgebaut hatte; und als sich die Überschwemmung endlich verlief, da ließ sie im Volksbewußtsein einen starken Niederschlag von orientalischen Vorstellungen zurück, der niemals wieder völlig verschwand.

Ich glaube damit zur Genüge gezeigt zu haben, inwiefern der Gegenstand, den ich zu behandeln versuchte, eine eingehendere Untersuchung verdiente. Obwohl mich das Studium desselben in jeder Beziehung viel weiter geführt hat, als ich anfangs vorauszusehen vermochte, so sind mir die Arbeits- und Reisejahre doch nicht leid, welche ich ihm widmen mußte. Daß die Aufgabe, welche ich zu lösen hatte, eine schwierige war, stellte sich bald genug heraus. Einerseits wissen wir nicht, in welchem Grade das Avesta und die anderen heiligen Bücher der Parsen den Vor-

— IV —

is that the Iranian and the Greco-Latin worlds, separated as much by instinctive antipathy as by hereditary enmity, remained perpetually averse to mutual assimilation.

Nevertheless, the religion of the magi, which represents the most perfect creation of the Iranian genius, influenced Western culture three times. First, <term>Parsism</term> <gloss>Persian religion</gloss> exerted a very noticeable effect on the emergence of Judaism, and some of its main teachings spread through the mediation of Jewish colonies throughout the entire Mediterranean basin and were later adopted by Catholic orthodoxy.

<term>Mazdaism</term> acted more directly upon the European world of thought once Rome had conquered the eastern part of Asia Minor. From time immemorial, colonies of magi who had emigrated from Babylon lived there in quiet seclusion, and in these barbaric regions, by weaving their traditional beliefs with Hellenic ideas, they had in time developed a cult that was original despite its complex nature. At the beginning of our era, one saw it suddenly emerge from the darkness and advance simultaneously in the Danube and Rhine valleys and into the heart of Italy. The peoples of the Occident felt deeply that the Mazdean faith was superior to their old national religions, and the masses streamed to the altars of the foreign god. But the progress of the conqueror stalled as soon as he came into contact with Christianity. With astonishment, the two opponents perceived how similar they were in many respects, without being able to account for the causes of this similarity. And for this reason, they accused the spirit of lies of having wanted to parody their holy customs. The conflict between the two was inevitable and became a heated, irreconcilable struggle, for its stake was world domination. No one has reported to us its changing moments, and our

Dennoch hat die Religion der Magier, welche die vollendetste Schöpfung des iranischen Genius darstellt, dreimal die abendländische Kultur beeinfluſt. Zunächst übte der Parsismus eine sehr merkliche Wirkung auf die Entstehung des Judentums aus, und einige seiner Hauptlehren verbreiteten sich durch Vermittelung der jüdischen Kolonieen im ganzen Mittelmeerbecken und wurden später von der katholischen Orthodoxie übernommen.

Unmittelbarer wirkte der Mazdaismus auf die europäische Gedankenwelt, als Rom den Osten Kleinasiens erobert hatte. Seit unvordenklicher Zeit lebten dort in stiller Verborgenheit Kolonieen von Magiern, die aus Babylon ausgewandert waren und in diesen barbarischen Gegenden, indem sie ihre traditionellen Glaubensvorstellungen mit hellenischen Ideen verwoben, mit der Zeit einen trotz seiner komplexen Beschaffenheit originellen Kultus herausgebildet hatten. Am Anfang unserer Zeitrechnung sah man ihn plötzlich aus dem Dunkel auftauchen und gleichzeitig im Donau- wie im Rheintal und bis in das Herz Italiens vordringen. Die Völker des Abendlandes empfanden tief, daſs der mazdäische Glaube ihren alten Nationalreligionen überlegen war, und die Massen strömten zu den Altären des fremden Gottes. Aber die Fortschritte der Eroberers stockten, sobald er mit dem Christentum Fühlung bekam. Mit Erstaunen gewahrten die beiden Gegner, wie ähnlich sie sich in vieler Hinsicht waren, ohne sich von den Ursachen dieser Ähnlichkeit Rechenschaft geben zu können. Und darum klagten sie den Geist der Lüge an, daſs er ihre heiligen Bräuche habe parodieren wollen. Der Konflikt zwischen beiden war unvermeidlich und wurde zu einem heißen, unversöhnlichen Kampfe, denn sein Einsatz war die Weltherrschaft. Niemand hat uns seine wechselnden Momente berichtet, und unsere

It is a most powerful affection, which renders lovers distracted and alters them so much that you would not recognize them as the same people. Some who suffer from insane love, however, love more impotently and consistently act less correctly by reason. Although these are led away from the right and the good by the impulse of love, they do not entirely wander in their mind, insofar as they know and acknowledge that what they are doing is less than right; nevertheless, they yield to the magnitude of the affection, see the better things, and approve of the worse. Eventually, the magnitude of the affection reaches such a point that, because of the continuous passions—by which they are vexed without any intermission—worry, sadness, cares, and anger, they finally wander entirely from reason.

From the thesis just presented, it becomes manifest that Melancholy does not arise immediately from imagination alone (as many falsely persuade themselves) but through the mediation of the generation of melancholic humor. ### CONCERNING HETEROCLITE NOUNS

Since there are certain nouns which are declined variably, which for that reason the Greeks call <term>heteroclita</term> <gloss>irregularly inflected</gloss>, and we call them heteroclite by a Greek name, because we do not have a Latin one: it seems worthwhile in this place to write about heteroclites, if I first specify that some nouns are <term>aptota</term> <gloss>indeclinable</gloss>. Which run uniformly through all cases, such as frugi <gloss>frugal/useful</gloss>, nequam <gloss>worthless</gloss> and similar ones, and the names of numbers, from four up to one hundred. Some are <term>monoptota</term> <gloss>having one case</gloss>, which have only one case, such as sponte <gloss>by one's own will</gloss>. And indeed, those who have believed that men initially crawled forth from the earth as a mute and base herd could scarcely have handed down anything else concerning the origin of languages. Therefore we, to whom the origin of the human race is more correctly open from the sacred codex, assert truly that the primordial language was infused into the first men, unless perhaps you wish to accept what Cratylus argues to the contrary in Plato, which is altogether vain and has already been exploded by others at greater length. Yet, although, as we mentioned above, we acknowledge the diversity of languages through a divine miracle because of the building of the Babylonian tower, nevertheless, since the mutual communication of duties among the human race must be exercised in every age, a convention could not but be entered into among diverse mortals, so that each one might use his faculty of speaking in a uniform way, and express the same things with the same words. Otherwise, there would be no use of speech, unless it were understood by both sides. ## TH. X.

Nor does it stand against this that a private individual is permitted to lose his own life for a King, Elector, or Christian prince established in danger of life, if he can save him. Which deed we read was done by Ribiscius, servant of Mauritius, D.S. Answer: This deed is not to be called <term>αὐτοχειρία</term> <gloss>suicide</gloss>; but it is founded in the dictate of right reason and love toward the public good: And it has as its primary end <term>καλόν τι</term> <gloss>a certain good/virtue</gloss>, that is, the preservation of common utility.

## TH. X. <note>sic, original repeats thesis number</note>

Nor does it stand against this that they object that it is *permitted* for a person invaded by someone to lose their own life, so that the soul of the invader might be freed. For I deny that this is permitted to the invaded, unless the aggressor is a person useful to the republic and the invaded a vile person; or if he is in danger of damnation: *as the Blessed Hülsemann once felt in the Treatise on the Law and Moderation of Correction.*

## TH. XII.

Nor does it stand against this that it is permitted for a common soldier to face inevitable danger of life for his Colonel, so that he might remain safe. For a great bond, such as a <term>Sacramentum</term> <gloss>oath of military allegiance</gloss>, obligates the soldier, by which he promised that he would promote the increase of the army and defend his safety, which in large part hangs from the safety of the Colonel.

## TH. XIII.

The other QUESTION is, *whether the companions lawfully slaughtered a willing and joyous companion, so that their own lives might be preserved?* which we again deny.

## TH. XIV.

For we rightly urge the divine command on not killing, which the omnipotent legislator gave to us. And it is agreed among those who recall the acts of men to the tribunal of conscience that only that can be held for a lawful cause of killing a man which God approved in his law as just, either expressly or by evident consequence. However, that the proposed case is excepted anywhere in the command of not killing, it is scarce possible to prove with a suitable argument.
