## TH. X.

Nec obstat, quod privato liceat pro Rege, Electore, aut principe Christiano in vitæ periculo constituto vitam propriam amittere, si illam servare possit. Quod quidem factum legimus à Ribiscio, Mauritii D. S. Famulo. Resp. Hoc factum non est αὐτοχειρία dicendum; sed fundatur in dictamine rectæ rationis & amore erga bonum publicum: Et pro fine primario habet καλόν τι h.e. communis utilitatis conservationem.

<note>The following heading is printed as TH. X., repeating the previous number, though logically it corresponds to thesis XI.</note>

## TH. X.

Nec obstat, quod objiciant, invaso ab aliquo vitam propriam amittere *licere*, ut invasoris anima liberetur. Nam nego hoc licere invaso, nisi aggressor aut sit persona reip. utilis & invasus persona vilis; aut in damnationis periculo versetur: *ut B. Hülsemannus in Tract. de Jure & Moderat. corrept. olim sensit.*

## TH. XII.

Nec obstat, quod militi gregario pro Chiliarchâ suo periculum vitæ adire inevitabile liceat, ut ille salvus maneat. Nam obligat militem vinculum aliquod magnum, Sacramentum puta, quô incrementum exercitûs promoturum, salutemque ejus, quæ magnâ ex parte ex salute Chiliarchæ pendet, defensurum promisit.

### THESIS XXIII.

Nam factum eorum tùm erat absolutè coactum à famis atrocitate et ventre auribus carente, ita, ut si extra hunc necessitatis casum fuisset, ad tale facinus non fuissent prolapsi ; tùm cum summâ quoque perturbatione animi conjunctum, qui non poterat facilè circumstantias facti perpendere, sed singulis mortem momentis anxius metuebat.

### THESIS XXIII.

Nec finis pœnarum acquiri poterat, sive emendationem lædentium spectes, qui tale quid extra necessitatis casum non ampliùs erant facturi ; sive satisfactionem pro læso, qui non ampliùs aderat ; sive præcautionem omnium, ut cautiùs mercarentur, quibus necessitatis hic casus vix timendus erat.

### THESIS XXIV.

Nec obstat, quod dicant quidam, in iis delictis, quæ pœnâ capitali coërcere Deus mandavit, quale est homicidium, non licere Majestati veniam dare. Respondeo. Circumstantiæ delicti sunt respiciendæ, ob quas Majestas civilis pœnas legibus determinatas immutare, mitigare, et exacerbare potest. Quô in casu non tam dispensatorem agit Majestas civilis, quàm interpretem, et non tam mitigat pœnam, quàm justè applicat. *Dominus Zieglerus. Dissertatio 4. de Jure Majestatis paragrapho 26.*

### THESIS XXV.

Neque tamen judicem in eo defenderim, quod nullô eos modô puniverit. Ad minimùm cum pœnam ordinariam haud adeò citra rationem ultrò ipsis remiserit, modô tamen extraordinariô punire eos debuisset cùm tàm atroci huic commisso homicidio pœnæ magis mitigatio, quàm totalis remissio conveniat. *vide Dominum Röhrensee in dicto casu paragrapho 23.*

one may proceed, there are to be brought into counsel (a) prudent men; (b) the architects of new exactions (c) and impostors (d) are by no means to be admitted. These prepare destruction for their councils, for the Republic, and for themselves (e).

(a) *It is an old saying that two eyes see more than one.* He who denies that this also applies to the Prince is ignorant that extreme talents are often raised to the throne: and that these, whether by age, or training, or nature, lack that first share of spirit and talent; or that the mind of one man is not capable of such a burden. Therefore, a Prince doubtful of the causes for imposing collections should take Counselors into these cares: and have their advice. *For those things which are managed by counsel are cared for better than those which are managed without counsel.* (b) We wish them to be prudent, that is, knowledgeable of the customs and spirits of the province, and of all things which Besoldus recounts at length, book 2, politics, chapter 4, page 687; furthermore, prompt in talent, and for whom advice is easy to draw from necessity, and is born under the hand. In such a case, let them first attempt everything that will help the Prince before the subsidy of the subjects. For it is not always impossible. Talent is effective when you apply it. Nor was the advice given to Claudius long ago, when he was complaining about the smallness of the treasury, absurd: *it would abound if it were received into partnership by two freedmen.* Those men were Pallas and Narcissus, the ones in charge of accounts, whom he had allowed to acquire and plunder much. *Suetonius, Claudius, chapter 28; Tacitus, 14 Annals, page 157.* (e) Although it is difficult and harsh to give counsel to a king, or to any mortal whose wealth is in the heights, it is nevertheless hardly considered by those who promise golden mountains to Princes. ### LXXX.

Nam cum constitutor simpliciter promittat se soluturum, quod
vel ipse vel alius debet: manifestum est, eum obligari citra solem-
nitatem verborum, neque iudicium eludere posse per exceptionem
viciosae stipulationis, sufficienti actori simplici pactione, quae prae-
cedenti obligationi innitatur, & hoc praetoris beneficio vestiatur.

### LXXXI.

Vnde manifeste elucet huius actionis a fideiussoria diuersitas,
cum fideiussor solemni stipulatione obligetur, & absque ea conue-

deiussoribus & <term>legem</term> stipulationum aliae, § satis acceptio, <term>Digestis</term> de <term>verborum obligationibus</term>
cum similibus.

### LXXXII.

Nouatione autem potior est constitutio, quod haec priorem
obligationem non tollat, quod illa facit: & cum alius pro alio con-
stituit, vterque obligatur, quod in nouationem non cadit, quo-
niam ea personam non mutat.

### LXXXIII.

Nudum autem pactum Ecclesiasticorum ex <term>capitulo primo extra de pactis</term>
huius actionis utilitatem non eleuat, quoniam id in forum ciuile,
receptiori calculo non recipitur, & denunciationes canonum mul-
tis in locis hodie contemnuntur: ubi vero earum adhuc ratio habe-
tur, ibi cum dicto pacto concurrit haec actio ciuilis, & vincit sociam
loco & modo proponendi.

### LXXXIIII.

Quemadmodum etiam prior obligatio multis de causis debi-
lior esse potest, quam ea quae oritur ex constituto, quod haec illi vel
ratione loci, vel temporis, vel alterius alicuius qualitatis & circum-
stantiae emolumenti aliquid addat. Et vt aliquando nihil fit in con-
stituto amplius, quam in praecedenti obligatione, utique tamen &
eo casu sua ipsi constat utilitas. Quod expediat actori, Reum pluri-
bus actionibus obnoxium tenere, & ex ijs vtram velit, posse eligere.

### LXXXV.

Et quamuis in formula tantum pecuniae mentio fiat, tamen ea
appellatio ad omnes res tam mobiles quam immobiles nunc perti-
net, ex receptitia iam antiquata huc transfusas, non ad eas tantum,

### LXXXVI.

Actionem de constituta pecunia sequitur apud Iustinianum: actio de peculio, quam praetor aequitate naturali motus introduxit, ne penitus ludificarentur ii, qui cum seruis aut filiis familias contrahunt, quibus domini, vel patres permittunt in rebus peculiaribus negotiari.

### LXXXVII.

Peculium autem nomen quidem habet a pecunia, quasi pusilla pecunia, id est pusillum patrimonium paragrapho ultimo Digesta eodem Sed interdum sumitur etiam pro quolibet cuiuslibet patrimonio lex cogit Digesta ad Trebellianum. Nonnunquam quoque pro pecunia praesidii causa reposita, unde dici solet, pecunia sine peculio fragilis lex si chorus paragrapho 1. Digesta de legatis 3 In hac tamen actionis forma, peculium in ea significatione accipitur, quae primo a nobis loco posita est.

### LXXXVIII.

Vt peculium sit, id quod filius familias vel seruus permissu patris vel domini, habet peculiare, separatum a rationibus paternis vel dominicis, eo deducto quod patri vel domino, vel iis qui in eorum potestate, tutela curaue sunt, debetur lex peculium, et lex sequens paragrapho ultimo Digesta de peculio.

### LXXXIX.

Non quod necesse esse putemus ut dominus vel pater semper concedant iis quos in potestate habent peculium, quoniam eo pacto filius furiosi, et seruus pupilli, vel furiosi peculium non haberent; sed quod cum Iuliano satis esse putemus, eiusmodi personas peculium iis non adimere, quibus priores domini vel patres ante concessissent lex quam Tuberonis Digesta de peculio.

### LXXXX.

Quamuis autem tam feruis quam filiis familias: peculium attribuimus non tamen eodem modo utrisque: cum seruorum peculium uniforme sit, filiorum vero quadripartitum prout a diuersis causis proficiscitur, a patre vel eius intuitu aliunde, aut simpliciter aliunde, aut ab industria militari, vel quasi.

### LXXXXI.

Neque tamen ad omnes has species accommodata est haec actio, sed ad profectitium tantum: quoniam in castrensi vel quasi filius-familias

### LXXIIII.

That seems to us to be of civil rigor rather than natural equity, that in not acquiring, the fraud of the debtor is unpunished and does not give place to this action.

### LXXV.

In which species, if an heir or co-legatee colludes with the debtor, we assert that it is consistent with equity that a Christian judge can admit the useful <term>Pauliana</term>, or at least, by disguising the name of the action, provide the same effect to the creditor, by the argument of the law 3, Digest, title *siquid in fraudem patronorum.*

### LXXVI.

Especially when we know that the fraudulent acquisition of a debtor is not usually to the fraud of creditors, as in the law 1, § *sed si emerit*, Digest, title *siquid in fraudem patronorum.*

### LXXVII.

Regarding the time and exercise of the <term>Pauliana</term>, we feel with those who establish a year from the beginning as useful, then continuous, so that however the fraudulent profit can be sought back perpetually, by the argument of the law *ait praetor*, 2 response, penultimate paragraph, Digest, title *quae in fraudem.*

### LXXVIII.

But of the <term>Pauliana</term>, enough has been said for our institute. Another example of a praetorian personal action is in <term>Iustinianus</term>: *de constituta pecunia* <gloss>concerning money promised</gloss>, which although some think is superfluous today for various reasons, and therefore useless, we nevertheless agree with others who affirm that the convenience and use of this action still remain with us in many ways.

### LXXIX.

Not indeed that the constitution does not often fall into other forms of actions, and sometimes concurs as if with a stipulation, sometimes with suretyship, sometimes with novation, sometimes even with a bare pact, often dressed in a diverse reason; and it always arises from a preceding obligation, which without a new constitution would supply its own action for demanding what is owed to each; but because the constitution always enriches and affects the prior action with a new benefit and convenience, so that it differs in something from the other already mentioned forms of actions, and has and protects its own ends and terms.

### LXXIIII.

Illud nobis rigoris civilis potius esse videtur, quam aequitatis naturalis, quod in non acquirendo debitoris fraus sit impunis, & huic actioni locum non faciat.

### LXXV.

In qua specie, si cum debitore colludat haeres vel collegatarius, Christianum iudicem utilem Paulianam admittere posse, vel saltem dissimulato nomine actionis, eundem effectum creditori praestare, aequitati consentaneum esse asserimus, argumento lex 3. Digestum siquid in fraudem patronorum.

### LXXVI.

Praesertim cum sciamus fraudulentam debitoris acquisitionem creditoribus fraudi esse non solere lex 1. § sed si emerit, Digestum siquid in fraudem patronorum.

### LXXVII.

De tempore & exercitio Paulianae, sentimus cum iis, qui annum à principio utilem statuunt, deinde continuum, ut tamen fraudulentum lucrum perpetuò repeti possit, argumento lex ait praetor, 2. responsum § penultima Digestum quae in fraudem.

### LXXVIII.

Sed de Pauliana iam, pro nostro instituto, satis multa. Alterum exemplum actionis praetoriae personalis est apud Iustinianum: de constituta pecunia, quam etsi putant quidam varijs de causis esse hodie superfluam, idcircò inutilem, nos tamen alijs astipulamur, qui huius actionis commoditatem & usum multis modis adhuc nobis constare affirmant.

### LXXIX.

Non quidem quod non saepè in alias actionum formas incidat constitutum, & modo cum stipulatione, modo cum fideiussione, modo cum novatione, etiam cum pacto aliquando nudo, saepè diversa ratione vestito, quasi concurrat: semperque ex praecedenti obligatione oriatur, quae citra novam constitutionem, suam ipsa actionem suppeditet ad exigendum quod cuique debetur; sed quod constitutio priorem actionem novo semper beneficio & commodo ita locupletet & afficiat, ut à caeteris iam nominatis actionum formis in aliquo differat, ac proprios fines & terminos habeat atque tueatur.

Germany, the broadest of all European provinces, a fertile region and overflowing with illustrious and strenuous men, has always been held in great esteem. Having obtained this as his homeland, the Illustrious Baron was brought forth into the light at GERA in the year 1572, on the 10th day of June, two months after his Generous father had ceased to be among the living. The death of his parent had extorted such great weeping and groaning from everyone that the most bitter mourning seemed to dwell in the whole court, in the whole city, and in the whole territory of the Reuss <term>Rutheno</term> <gloss>of the Reuss family</gloss>. But as soon as that Generous posthumous child was born, everyone suddenly began to exult with joy and openly triumph with gladness; everyone raised a sign, as it were, to hope well for the Republic. For the condition of mortals has these changes, that joyful things are substituted for sad ones, and adverse things are mingled with favorable ones, lest sorrow lack a remedy, and joy be devoid of discipline.

Why should I now commemorate the illustrious Reuss family, whose names are bound by a long order and many foldings of coats of arms? This family is most noble both by itself, through its antiquity and the glory of its ancestors, and the more noble in that it has long since bound itself with manifold affinity not only with very many Counts and Barons, but also with the most powerful Dukes of Pomerania, Mecklenburg, and Hesse. Much less should it be supposed that they lay alive and breathing in open tombs throughout the three days that Christ spent in the sepulcher, until they came forth after the resurrection of the Lord; rather, it is credible that the tombs remained broken open for those three days until the soul was reunited with the body.

§ 11. For after the resurrection of the Savior, the resurrected ones went out from their tombs and came into the holy city, as the text clearly asserts. For those words <term>μετὰ τὴν ἔγερσιν αὐτοῦ</term> <gloss>after his resurrection</gloss> pertain not only to the going forth, but also to the resurrection of those saints, in that those saints were both resurrected and immediately went out from the tombs after the resurrection of Christ. Nor is it an obstacle that the Evangelist does not recount this resurrection of the saints after the history of the resurrection of Christ, but rather before it. For he does this by means of <term>ὕστερον πρότερον</term> <gloss>placing the latter first</gloss>, on the occasion of the remaining miracles that occurred after the death of Christ. Divine Jerome says that these saints did not therefore rise before the Lord, even though their tombs were opened, so that the Savior might be the firstborn of the resurrection from the dead, as he is called in Colossians chapter 1, verse 18, and Revelation chapter 1, verse 5. But because some were resurrected even in the Old Testament before Christ, and indeed by Christ himself in the days of his flesh, Christ is therefore called the firstborn of the dead or from the dead, not so much in respect of time as in respect of eminence, power, and efficacy, because Christ not only rose by his own power, but also by his resurrection is not merely an example, but is also the cause of the resurrection of others to blessed life.

FACTUM Appii illius, qui caecus fuit, magna in laude pono. (Patres et Collegae excellentissimi.) Is audito de grauissimo negotio in Curia tractatum iri, eo se deferri voluit, vt periclitanti patriae consilio succurreret: Imitarer etiam quod laudo, nisi me valetudo, senectus et vocis imbecillitas impediret. Neque enim minor est mihi cura Venetiarum quam Appio Romae, neque minus ego in mea Reipublicae sum uersatus quam ille in sua. En Chrysippeum Deum tam invalidum, ut nec hominem morborum expertem fingere potuerit, utut voluerit. Materia illi capistrum injecit. <margin>A</margin>De natura Pythagoras scribere adorsus esset, ita in principio dixerit, Non per aerem quem spiro, non per aquam quam bibo, non admittam huius sermonis vituperationem. Scripsit autẽ Pythagoras tria volumina, De institutione, De ciuilitate, De natura. Quod autem nomine Pythagoræ legitur, Lysidis Tarentini Pythagorici est, qui quum Thebas profugisset, Epaminondæ præceptor fuit. Refert Heraclides Serapionis filius in Sotionis Epitome, scripsisse & illum versibus De toto. Secundum item Sacrum sermonem, cuius est initium,

Tertium De anima: quartum De pietate: quintum Helothalem Epicharmi comici patrem: sextum Crotonem & alios. Porrò mysticum sermonem aiunt Hippasi fuisse, qui in iniuriam Pythagoræ scripserit, plura item ab Astone Crotoniate scripta Pythagoræ inscripta esse. Ait autem Aristoxenus complura moralium dogmatum accepisse Pythagoram à Themistoclea sorore. Ion autẽ Chius in Triaginis ait ipsum, quũ poema quoddam scripsisset, Orphei titulum adnotauisse. <margin>C</margin> Scopiadas itidem ipsius esse aiunt, cuius operis initium est, Nullius rex egens esto. Quemadmodum enim ad hanc alii certaturi, alii negotiaturi, alii optimi futuri spectatores veniunt, ita & in vitam alios quidem gloriæ mancipia nasci, & cupiditatis aucupes, <margin>312</margin> alios verò veritatis studiosos. Et ista quidem sic se habent. Verùm in tribus illis Pythagoræ opusculis quæ diximus, feruntur ista in vniuersum. <margin>A</margin>He descended into the Cave of Ida. In Egypt, he entered the inner sanctuaries, then returned to Samos, and finding his fatherland under the control of the tyrant <term>Polycrates</term>, he sought Croton in Italy. There he gave laws to the Italians and became famous along with his disciples, who numbered nearly three hundred and managed the republic in an outstanding manner, so prudently that it was deservedly seen as an <term>aristocratia</term> <gloss>republic of the best men</gloss>. <term>Heraclides Ponticus</term> reports that he was accustomed to say of himself that he had once been <term>Æthalides</term> and was considered the son of <term>Mercurius</term> <gloss>Mercury</gloss>, and that Mercury had advised him to ask for anything he wanted, except for immortality. Therefore, he asked that, both while living and after life had ended, he might retain the memory of everything that had happened. Thus, in life, he remembered all things. He also preserved the same memory after death, and some time later he entered into <term>Euphorbus</term> and was wounded by <term>Menelaus</term>. Now, <term>Euphorbus</term> said that he had once been <term>Æthalides</term> and had received from Mercury as a gift that his soul should wander in perpetual migration and pass into whatever trees or living creatures it wished, and that it should remember everything the soul had suffered in the underworld, and what the other souls suffered.

<margin>B</margin>

<margin>C</margin>After <term>Euphorbus</term> died, his soul entered <term>Hermotimus</term>, who himself, wishing to provide proof, went to the <term>Branchidae</term> <gloss>a priestly clan at Didyma</gloss> and, entering the temple of <term>Apollo</term>, pointed out the shield which <term>Menelaus</term> had affixed there. He says that when <term>Menelaus</term> had returned from Troy, he had dedicated to <term>Apollo</term> the shield, which was already rotting, and only the ivory face remained. When <term>Hermotimus</term> had finished his life, it migrated again into <term>Pyrrhus</term>, the Delian fisherman, and he remembered everything: that he had first been <term>Æthalides</term>, afterwards <term>Euphorbus</term>, then <term>Hermotimus</term>, and finally <term>Pyrrhus</term> was made, and then after <term>Pyrrhus</term> it became <term>Pythagoras</term>, and he remembered everything we have previously mentioned. Most say that <term>Pythagoras</term> wrote nothing, but they think this foolishly. For <term>Heraclitus</term> the physicist speaks about him most clearly: <term>Pythagoras</term>, son of <term>Mnesarchus</term>, practiced the study of history more than all other men, and selecting these writings, he created his own wisdom, much knowledge, and the study of the arts. <margin>L.</margin>
But this is not perpetual, for guardians appointed by testament, or by inquiry, are not burdened with the provision of security.

<margin>LI.</margin>
But if two or more are appointed by testament or inquiry, one may offer security for the indemnity of the minors, so that he alone may administer.

<margin>LII.</margin>
Unless a co-guardian or co-curator also offering security is preferred over him.

<margin>LIII.</margin>
Otherwise, if out of several no one offers security, if indeed the testator has written down who should act, he must act.

<margin>LIIII.</margin>
But if it has not been written, the one whom the majority elects shall administer.

<margin>LV.</margin>
But if the guardians themselves disagree regarding the election, the <term>Praetor</term> <gloss>a high-ranking Roman magistrate</gloss> is bound to intervene.

<margin>LVI.</margin>
Which we shall show, with the Emperor's authority, also holds true for several appointed by inquiry.

<margin>LVII.</margin>
Moreover, so that it might be better provided for minors and other persons, a <term>actio subsidiaria</term> <gloss>a subsidiary action</gloss> was invented against those who either failed to ensure that security was provided by the guardians or curators at all, or who allowed it to be provided inadequately. This, according to the Constitutions, is also extended to their heirs, by which it is also expressed that unless guardians and curators provide security, they should be restrained by the seizure of pledges.

<margin>LVIII.</margin>
Guardians and curators are, however, excused for various reasons.

<margin>LIX.</margin>
For instance, on account of the number of three, four, or five children.

Porphyry writes that when he had given diligent effort to astrology, and had finally seen through the vanity of the art and the falsity of its predictions, he revoked all faith in the astrologers. Therefore, in the book dedicated to him, titled *On the Efficiency of the Stars*, he laughed at and refuted the dogmas of the astrologers. Maternus, bearing this with difficulty, lies much about his death, as if he paid the penalty for his labor. For that it is most false is easily understood from Porphyry himself, the disciple of Plotinus, who faithfully describes the manner of his disease and death, and why and for what reason he left Rome. Diogenes Adamantius, in the philosophical sect, as in all disciplines most eminent, has often and many times refuted astrological vanity, unless perhaps his testimony is worth less because he is a Christian—but he was not a Christian. Eudorus, who also heard Plato and lived in Egypt and was considered the prince of astronomers in his time, left behind writing that nothing should be believed of the astrologers who predict the fates of men from their horoscopes. Alexander of Aphrodisias, a supreme authority in Aristotelian philosophy, in his book *On Fate* addressed to the Emperors Severus and Antoninus, rejected the necessity of fate and refuted astrological arguments. Perhaps he was drawn to mention fate only to correct the mind of Severus Caesar from such philosophical superstition. Averroes, a celebrated philosopher in the same family and a serious estimator of natural things, lacerates and attacks astrology everywhere. For in his first philosophy, he calls the astrological opinion about celestial images, under which earthly figures are thought to be subject to animals, fabulous, and with its removal, the greater part of astrological superstition falls. Similarly, explaining the *Cantica* of Avicenna, he says elsewhere that it is contrary to philosophy, and elsewhere that almost all the dogmas of the astrologers are false, and the art itself is entirely vain and weak. In his books against Algazel, he asserted that the artificial images, from which astrologers think they can derive the influence of the heavens, are inefficient. Avicenna, a great man in all disciplines, in the final book of his first philosophy, proved with many arguments that future things cannot be foreseen by astrologers. Therefore, no faith should be placed in their predictions. I omit Hericus from Asia and many other illustrious moderns who, in the Parisian academy, pursued this vanity in their dedicated works, and the greatest part of philosophers, who rather than refuting it, preferred to treat it like other deceitful arts, old wives' tales, and the ravings of illusionists. But it is worthy of note that even those who called themselves astronomers rejected this profession, which they could not do entirely without conscience and fear of falsity, since otherwise, they would have gained as much science, glory, and profit from the faith and authority of astrology as those who exercise themselves in the motions of the heavens. ## XVIIII.

Nec qualitates tantum necessarias comparat, verùm, si viuentis forma sit, decentem quoque molem temporis successu præbet. Ea moles cum accidens quoddam sit materiæ primæ inhærens, nec materia prima substantiali forma naturaliter carere possit: vnà cum molis accessione substantiam aliam atque aliam accedere atque aggenerari, & proinde nutritionem cum augmentatione dari necesse est, quam nutritionem accidentali solùm dissidio à generatione distingui certum est.

## XX.

Quædam digesto intus alimento, quædam foris præparato nutriuntur. Quæ intus alimentum digerunt, os minimum & ingluuiem quandam seu ventrem habeant necesse est. Animalium Perfectorum plæraque etiam ventriculum, intestinum, hepar & venas obtinent. Ventriculus delapsum ex ore cibum fibrarum obliquarum ministerio ita complectitur, vt necesse sit indigestum è piloro sese proripere, nisi prouida natura glandulosis quibusdam tuberculis id impediret.

## XXI.

Extemplò coquens facultas, quæ est stomachi ipsius substantiæ identificata, adhibito calore vt instrumento præcipuo gnauitèr in concoctionem incumbit, hepate, liene, diaphragmate, corde, opus hinc inde urgentibus. perfecto opere pilorus panditur, chylusque intestinum duodenum ingrediens rectà ad crassum adeoque crassi intestini partem extremam, quæ aluus dicitur, vergit, ac sese intestina flexuosis anfractibus decurrendo osculis mesaraicarum frequentissimis exsugendum præbet, ita vt præter fæces retineat nihil.

## XXII.

Succum & florem chyli venæ Mesaraicæ per Mesenterium ad portam deferunt, ex qua confestim attrahente qualibet iecoris parte multiplicibus atque angustis ramis in vniuersum dissipatur iecur, ibique chymi seu quatuor humorum confectionem subit, ita vt è partibus calidioribus flaua, è frigidioribus magisque terreis atra bilis, è temperatioribus & subtilioribus sanguis, è minus subtilibus pituita generetur.

## XXIII.

Quatuor humores, vt specie & natura discrepant, ita non eidem omnes muneri sunt deputati. Flaua enim bilis folliculo caua iecoris parte suspenso excipitur, inde in duodenum intestinis sua acrimonia pur-

### XXIIII.

Dehinc in omnes corporis partes, tàm heterogeneas, quàm homogeneas, ad quascunque aliquis patet accessus, vehente pituita mæandris venarum propè innumeris inenarrabili penitus ratione defertur. Quod enim maximè familiare cuiuis est parti, id aut vltrò adnatat, aut à virtute trahente eminus inuitatur atque attrahitur.

### XXV.

Pituita intereà sanguinis naturam induit ex parte, reliquum venas emunctorias, inde renes, tandem vesicam subit, & in lotium vertitur. Ea demum concoctio, quæ in omnibus viuentis partibus exercetur, & qua sanguis formâ suâ relictâ in substantiam animalis abit, est nutritio, cui si non tantum augmentatio, sed etiam rarefactio sit comes, animal in ampliorem fundet molem, aliâs nequaquam.

### XXVI.

Cùm autem viuentis partes rarescunt, non nouam aliquam quantitatem, sed vbi duntaxat nouum vetere abiecto acquirunt, excrementitium vaporem exhalant, poros laxant, & largiùs alimentum imbibunt. Vacuum, vt naturæ viribus vniuersè dari nequit, ita nec rarescentibus viuentis partibus importatur.

### XXVII.

Augmentatio viuentis secundum formale significatum est actio, qua alimenti quantitas viuentis quantitati nectitur, estque aut eiusdem virtutis actio, cuius est nutritio, quam virtutem à substantia viuentis non nisi ratione distinguimus, aut alterius, quam vnionibus materiæ primæ identificatam esse arbitramur.

### XXVIII.

Fieri tàm augmentatio, quàm nutritio partium singularum continuè potest, & quidem toto vitæ tempore, nisi morbi aliaque id genus incommoda sese ingerant, & quasi nutritionis atque augmentationis filum scindant. ### XV.

Like can usually generate like, but sometimes it cannot; therefore, a living thing is sometimes produced from a dissimilar living thing, but never from a non-living thing. Angels can produce only local motion, and perhaps also impetus, which is sometimes the main cause of the same motion; it is so far from the case that they create a living thing or any other substance. The same thing in number cannot be produced naturally again, or twice; it can be produced divinely.

### XVI.

Now it is certainly clear that generation is an action entirely different from alteration, and that generation is said to be the limit of alteration very improperly. For how, since it is an action, can it terminate alteration? And how is it not different from alteration, when it has a different limit? The formal limit of generation, in man, is indeed the union of the individual and spiritual rational soul with the divisible and material, and in all others, besides union, also divisible forms: but the ultimate and adequate limit is the whole composite.

### XVII.

Whence it is rightly defined by the Philosopher as the change of the whole into the whole, with no sensible subject remaining the same. For the whole composite is truly generated, and since prime matter can naturally support only a single substantial form—and that of some lowest species—the whole substantial composite that was before, or the sensible subject, must perish. From which it is plain that every generation which is comprehended by this definition is a certain conversion, although not every generation is absolutely a conversion, nor is every conversion a generation. For the former cannot be given outside a subject, and the latter cannot be given from a privative or negative limit.

### XVIII.

But the subject of generation is prime matter alone, endowed with quantity and other accidents, which it is not necessary to perish at the very moment of generation, since they are neither stripped of their subject, nor abandoned by their preserving cause, nor are they judged to perish by the entire and uncorrupted judgment of the senses. §. 3. I come to the celebrants themselves of this Pseudo-Jubilee, some of whom are living in Rome, or are merely present there at that time, while others are absent. Those who travel to Rome themselves are received with a great display of honor; graces are provided for them for their arrival, because they did not hesitate to celebrate this Festival, having left their native Churches for that City in which (if it is permitted to believe) the keys of the Kingdom of Heaven are, and that inexhaustible Treasury of the Church, whose Guardian and Dispenser is the Roman Pontiff, as Marchantius describes Rome in his *Hortus Pastorum* <gloss>Garden of Pastors</gloss>. Furthermore, the most plenary indulgence, remission, and pardon of all sins is promised to them, with this condition added: if they are to visit the Basilicas of the Blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, St. John Lateran, and St. Mary Major, as the Bulls of the Pontiffs expressly hold. Before Boniface VIII, indeed, as Prosius notes, those who came to Rome for the sake of the Jubilee were held to visit only the Church of St. Peter; but with the passage of time, they were bound to the others as well. For in addition to the Church of St. Peter, which had to be approached, Boniface VIII later added that of St. Paul, Clement VI that of St. John Lateran, and Gregory XI that of St. Mary Major: as if, in truth, divine Grace were to be sought in these temples in particular, when nevertheless our Savior, making no respect for this or that place, says: *Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them, Matth. 18:20.* These Churches must be visited repeatedly according to the number of days prescribed by the Roman Pontiff, which, unless it is fulfilled by those blind celebrants, there is no reason, as they say, for anyone to promise oneself the most plenary pardon of one's transgressions. Thus, the Bull of Urban VIII holds:

> *To those who devoutly visit the Lateran Church, the Basilicas of the Blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, and also St. Mary Major of the City, at least once a day for thirty continuous or interrupted days if they are Romans or Inhabitants of the City, or if they are pilgrims or otherwise foreigners, for at least fifteen days, and who pour out pious prayers to GOD for the salvation of those faithful and the whole Christian people, we mercifully in the Lord grant and impart the most plenary Indulgence, remission, and pardon of all their sins.*

To follow the examples of this man and of similar ones—Scaevola, Crassus, Sulpicius, who avoided no labor of teaching even when established in the highest dignities—is also honorable and distinguished for our Jurists, and let them know that this duty of interpreting laws and assiduity in judgments is not only full of dignity, but also pleasing to God.

### Regarding the character and life of Papinian, it shall be judged from his writings.

For speech is the index of the mind, and we willingly and frequently speak of those things which settle in our hearts: as the Poet says:

> The sailor speaks of winds, the plowman of bulls
> The soldier counts his wounds, the shepherd his sheep.

So also our Jurists have written the best precepts of life and rules for living honestly, for harming no one, and for giving each his own, to which we ought to refer and derive all our actions of life as if to a norm. Their character and life were consistent with these precepts. For they themselves wished to invite other men to the reverence of laws and the love of justice by their own example.

Such was Neratius Priscus, whose life was equal to his precepts. Such was his probity, such his loyalty, candor, integrity of character, such his wisdom and moderation in judging, and his love of justice and equity, that he was even to the most lauded Emperor Trajan

The proper sensible aspect is color and light, although light is also an extrinsic condition of the medium, and indeed is necessary solely for the vision of any external object. Color, as it is visible, is defined by Aristotle in Book 2 of On the Soul, text 67, as the mover of that which is actually transparent; and in Chapter 3 of On Sense and the Sensible, as the extremity of the transparent in a bounded body. As a thing, color can be defined as a simple quality, distinct in reality and essence from external light, resulting immediately from light, transparency, and elementary opacity tempered together, and mediately from a certain temperature of the four primary qualities. The medium of sight is anything transparent, yet it is so simply and in every dimension that is permeable to light. The organ is that certain part of the eye which is called the pupil.

### <term>Protrepticus</term> <gloss>Exhortation</gloss> of Eobanus Hessus for servants

Hidden in servitude, to show yourself a faithful servant,
You who wish for this, read through whatever is here with you.
The first law commands the faith of a servant to be kept,
Beware of trusting words to things.
A good man abstains from the master's things, be diligent,
And do not carry your body at a tortoise's pace.
Wanton impudence has made many fall from grace,
You can be praised for learned simplicity.
Let him avoid gamblers. Let him not be a boaster. And everyone
Who flees the one who has become like an abyss, he is wise.
He will carry out commands quickly: let him not murmur against them: let there be absent
From the servant laughter and immoderate jests.
Hear much: do not speak much unless asked.
He whom you see to be dear to the master, cultivate.
Let you not seem a biting critic of anyone's infamy: but be devoid
Of envy. Flee lawsuits and discord.
Let frequent care make you teachable, lest soft
Leisure make you hard: accustom yourself to be pressed by labor.
Whoever is an adulator is not held faithful to the master,
The law also forbids drunken wine to servants.

If you note any by chance: pretend you do not know.

seed: After the light of the following day had removed the shadow from the earth, the priest approached the solemn altar in the manner of a suppliant, and scarcely pours out the angelic melody from his breast, sweetly closing his eyes in his final life. ERMINOLD departs to inhabit the eternal seats. Therefore, hail thrice blessed, crowned with the wreath of martyrdom, hail, golden torch of the upper seat, hail again, most desired hope of the Bavarian land. Not because you are taken from us do you cease to be a help; a great part of you, your venerable body, a vessel without blemish sacred to GOD, offers remedies. For at your tomb various diseases are forced to depart; the plague, suddenly defeated, releases its foul scales and spots, and the elephantiasis <note>leprosy</note> introduced into the limbs stops the ulcers flowing with shedding pus. Now tongues that were bound, now the use of sight is restored; now suddenly those who were lame extend their steps with strengthened knees; moreover, the furies of Avernus <note>the underworld</note> are driven away, vexing the limbs of men with various torments. What? Am I silent or do I speak? The vows of no one are seen to be empty, whoever asks for help with a sound heart. But why am I, exhausted, finishing everything, carried in a small boat? Long ago Phoebus <note>the sun</note> ordered me to rest, so that I would not be overwhelmed by the burden. You, divine one, be mindful of your worshippers often, and favor the slight efforts of our labor, and favor us eternally.

# PRECETA LEGIS MOSAICE.
->In compendium redacta.<-

## PRECEPTVM .I.
### NON HABEBIS DEOS ALIENOS
Est timor Dei in amore, fide vera, spe solida, in rebus secundis & aduersis, ac vita denique vniuersa.

### REVS HVIVS PRECEPTI.
Qui vitam conditionemque suam, in omni fortunae habitu, alij, quam deo adscribit, in se aut suis, non deo confidit.

## PRECEPTVM .II.
### NON ADSVMES NOMEN DEI TVI
->Inuanum.<-
Est gloriam, honorem, benedictionem, deo referre, illum solum colere, quicquid boni habeas huic vni acceptum referre, illum inuocare, te ipsum detestari. Quicquid autem boni sit, dei nomen esse ambigit nemo.

### ILLIVS PRECEPTI REVS.
Qui in aliud, dei nomine, quam ad illius gloriam vtitur. Qui suo sibi aliquo bono blanditur, virtutem laudemque aliunde quam a deo quaerit.

## PRECEPTVM .III.
### SABBATA SANCTIFICES.
Est deo intendere, atque illius gratiam & solam appetere, ac inquirere.

### REVS.
Quicunque animo non feriatur deo, sacra luce operi, instat: diuina non curat, vel frigide curat: requiem, & a vicijs, sabbatum non colit.

## PRECEPTVM IIII
### HONORA PATREM ET MATREM.

Est animorum, sermonis, & operum puritas & verecundia, victus parsimonia, caelestium rerum illibatus amor, voluptatum contemptus, solius dei dilectio.

Quicunque voluptatibus dissoluuntur, risu & gaudio immodestius fruuntur, aut fruentes non cohibent frenantque. Quique aliarum rerum, quam dei curam animam agere permittunt.

Est omnis auaritiae fuga, laeta paupertas, liberalitas, humanitas.

## On the Chapel of Saint Nicholas for the youth of Freising.

If you, little boy, are not drawn to an age similar to your own,
And do not wish to be an emulator of the divine Nicholas;
Do not refuse to approach the nearby thresholds of Nicholas,
Let him at least attract you with his golden spheres.
You ask, I see no gifts of gold there; that is true;
For the Saint sees no one who seeks those things.

## Fountain of Saint Corbinian in Weyhenstephan.

Here where the slopes of the very high mount incline,
And the fountain flows of its own accord with scarcely any murmur,
By the impulse of his staff and prayers sent to the stars,
Corbinian produced flowing Waters.
This wave does not only remove thirst from those who thirst,
But, when drawn, it also often provides help to the sick.
Stop, Traveler, and drink this wave most eagerly,
Perhaps it also has within it that which may heal you.

## On the Chapel of Saint Corbinian built above the fountain.

The Chapel which was built for you at the base of the Mount,
Is ennobled by your waters, Corbinian.
Truly, this water is now drawn more often; therefore the Chapel
Has ennobled your waters, Corbinian.

### XLV.

<margin>Whether the sense of Scripture is obscure.</margin>
Their other objection also labours under no less futility, by which they clamour that Scripture is obscure, and therefore they do not admit just anyone to the reading of it.

### XLVI.

Although we cannot deny that CERTAIN passages in the Holy Scriptures are found to be more difficult and obscure to us, since the Lord Peter himself affirms that there are some such things in the Pauline Epistles. 2 Pet. 3:16.

### XLVII.

Nevertheless, we rightly conclude with the Lord Augustine that from these very obscurities nothing at all can be derived which has not been most plainly explained and resolved by the Holy Spirit in other, clearer passages of Scripture.

### XLVIII.

Therefore, although some obscure things are found in the Holy Code, the sense of Scripture itself is nonetheless clear and manifest, and all and singular articles of religion have open testimonies in the Scriptures.

### XLIX.

But such is the shame of the Papists, that they do not blush to accuse the mouth of divine Truth of lying, whereas Deut. 30:11 affirms that the commandment of God is not hidden, nor far off, but v. 14, very near.

### L.

Moreover, they resist David to his face, who in Ps. 19:8 affirms of the word of God that the commandment of the Lord is clear and enlightens the eyes, and in Ps. 119:105 says that it is a lamp to his feet and a light to his paths.

### LI.

And certainly, the Apostle Peter thinks far better and more honourably of it, whose successors the Roman Pontiffs falsely boast themselves to be, saying: We have a more sure prophetic word, to which you do well to pay attention, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in our hearts. 2 Peter 1:19.

But the law (as Varro elegantly wrote) neither disparages the innocent because of a feud, nor forgives the guilty because of friendship: but, as Cicero says, it speaks to all with one and a common voice. Which, however, some in Livy call into criticism, while saying that the King and the Law are contending with each other, they say that he is a man for whom there is room for favor and pardon; that this is a thing harsh and inexorable.

But also with sumptuary laws (which we know also existed among the Romans from Gellius and Macrobius), devised most ingeniously and skillfully, he chastised and repressed the luxury of citizens, and indeed of women most of all. For when most other legislators had imposed a pecuniary fine on those who had offended against sumptuary laws, Zaleucus did nothing of the sort; but he permitted everything to everyone only by applying disgraceful conditions. For he wanted it to be permitted for a woman to use gold in her adornment, and to be dressed in painted clothing, only if she wanted to be considered a prostitute by everyone. Honest matrons were to be clothed in simple dress and white garments. He ordered a free woman not to go out into public accompanied by more than one handmaiden, unless she wanted to appear drunk: nor did he permit her to go out at night, unless she wanted to be accused of lewdness. He forbade men, however, from wearing a gold ring and being clothed in Milesian garments, unless they wanted to be seen as followers of whores or lurkers in others' beds: just as Laertius book 1 also is the author that the Magi of the Persians forbade their people the outward cultivation and use of gold. By this method, however, Zaleucus achieved in a short time, and indeed without punishment, what others could scarcely achieve in a long time and with a heavy threatened penalty, that the citizens were dedicated to modesty and temperance. For who of an honest face would have wanted to expose himself to the laughter and mockery of all, as if the sign of his own disgrace were lifted? So also at Athens there was a law that only prostitutes should wear flowery and painted garments, as Suidas testifies: and it is certain that at Rome too, the habit of prostitutes and matrons was once different. For they used yellow clothing: so that of course, as Plautus testifies, the customs of a virgin diverge far from a "she-wolf," so also they might be distinguished from each other by their clothes themselves. Wherefore he who has attempted the chastity of a matron or virgin, when they were dressed in prostitute's clothing, is denied to be held for *iniuriarum* <gloss>damages for insults</gloss> by Ulpian in law 15, also among Labeo, section 15, *if one [violates] virgins*, <term>Digesto</term> <gloss>Digest</gloss> on insults.

Lex autem (vt eleganter *Varro* scripsit) neque innocenti propter simultatem obstringillat, neque nocenti propter amicitiam ignoscit: sed, vt ait *Cicero*, cum omnibus vna et communi voce loquitur. Quod tamen in reprehensionem vocant quidam apud *Liuium*, dum Regem ac Legem inter se contendentes, illum esse aiunt hominem, apud quem gratiae ac veniae locus sit; hanc esse rem duram atque inexorabilem.

Sed et sumptuariis legibus (quas aliquot etiam apud Romanos fuisse ex *Agellio* et *Macrobio* scimus) admodum ingeniose et solerter excogitatis luxuriam ciuium, et quidem foeminarum potissimum, castigauit ac repressit. Nam cum alij Legumlatores plerique multam irrogassent pecuniariam, qui in leges sumptuarias peccassent, nihil tale *Zaleucus*; sed turpibus tantum appositis condicionibus omnia omnibus permisit. Nam ita demum licere voluit mulieri aurum in mundo suo adhibere, et picta indui veste, si pro meretrice ab omnibus haberi vellet. Honestae matronae simplice cultu et veste candida amicirentur. Mulierem liberam non pluribus vna ancilla pedisequa et cognatis suis comitatam iussit in publicum prodire, nisi si ebria videri vellet: Neque noctu eam foras prodire permisit, nisi si probri insimulari vellet. Viris autem prohibuit annulum aureum gestare, et veste Milesia indui, nisi scortorum sectatores, aut alienorum subsessores cubilium videri vellent: quemadmodum et Magos Persarum exteriore cultu et vsu auri suis interdixisse, auctor est *Laertius libro 1.* Hac autem ratione *Zaleucus* id assecutus est breui, et quidem sine poena, quod alij vix longo tempore grauique interminata poena assequi potuerunt, vt ciues modestiae et temperantiae essent dediti. Quis enim integrae frontis quasi signo turpitudinis propriae sublato omnium sese risui ac ludibrio exponere voluisset? Sic et *Athenis* lex fuit, vt meretrices tantum gestarent vestes floridas et picturatas, teste *Suida*: Et *Romae* quoque olim diuersum fuisse meretricum et matronarum habitum constat. Illae enim lutea veste vtebantur: vt scilicet quemadmodum, *Plauto* teste, diuertunt mores *virgini* longe ac *lupae*, ita etiam vestibus ipsis inuicem discernerentur. Quare qui matronae aut virginis pudicitiam attentarit, cum eae meretricia veste indutae essent, iniuriarum teneri negatur ab *Vlpiano* in lege 15. item apud *Labeonem*. §. 15. *si quis virgines*. Digesto de iniuriis.

Verum omissis iam alijs *Zaleuci* legibus, ne nimium haec excrescat commentatio, vnam tantum postremo loco adiungam. Ea est, quam supra dixi proprio exemplo Legislatorem sanciuisse. Adulterij

In a short space of time, she finished these wars with nations skilled in arms; she came, she saw, she conquered: the limits of the dissertation and the meticulous harshness of wars forbid adding more. Finally, an emulator of either the power or the knowledge of the Indian King, she waged war against him, having been led to it by no just causes. She opposed the immense multitude of the Indian men with one million three hundred thousand infantry, five hundred thousand cavalry, and one hundred thousand chariots. She attempted to elude the elephants with a notable contrivance of ox-hides. Victorious at first in a naval battle, she then failed in the victory, having been overcome in a land battle by the betrayal of defectors and the simulation of the Indian King. She was also famous in internal wars. When it was announced to her, while she was occupied with the care of her hair, that Babylon had rebelled, she ran immediately to capture the city with one side of her hair still loose. Nor did she bring the beauty of her hair into order before she had brought such a city into her power. Therefore, her statue placed in Babylon is in that attire in which she hastened with precipitous speed to demand vengeance. ### XIV.

We must not omit in this place the most difficult question of this entire treatise, as Duarenus says, which few touch upon: Of what time must account be taken when one asks about the status, condition, and quality of the testator? We shall answer with a distinction.

<note>Supporting citations include: Institutes (on those not permitted), Digest, and commentaries by Duarenus, Donellus, and Vulteius.</note>

### XV.

The internal form of testaments is viewed in the institution of an heir, whence it is called the head and foundation of the testament, since without it nothing in it is valid, and it requires particular study.

Moreover, the customs and statutes of certain places have progressed so far that they make all goods, after entering the marriage bed, so communal that they are equally masters of them while the marriage exists, just as Carpzovius testifies regarding Saxon Law in Part 3, Constitution 25, Definition 6, Number 5.

### THES. VI.

By the appellation of Paraphernal Goods, as has been adduced in some way above, both movables and immovables, and debts owed, come under Law 7, Paragraph 3 of the Digest on the "Peculium" <gloss>private fund</gloss>, however they may have reached the wife before the marriage by civil law, whether by succession or by donation made by the husband himself to the bride (Law 5, Principle; Law 27; 32, Para. "if anyone a bride"; Law penultimate, Digest on donations between husband and wife). Through which, before the constitution of Constantine in Law 15, Code on donations before marriage, even if the marriage did not follow, things became the property of the recipient in such a way that they could not be alienated by the giver through a last will (Law last, Code on the same) or revoked if the marriage were dissolved (Law 12, Code on the same), nor could they be seized by the husband's creditors, unless he could prove that they were already obligated to him (Law 13, Code on the same). Which effects, however, today obtain only if the marriage has followed, per the said Law 15; see Corvinus on the same. Moreover, donations made while the marriage exists, in those cases where there is a place for donation between spouses (some of which are enumerated in Law 15, Para. 1; Law 25, Digest on donations between husband and wife; Law 11, Code on the same), can be added to Paraphernalia. To which donations is rightly referred today a donation celebrated on the Feast of the Nativity of Christ, just as universal Germany...

Moreover, reader, seeking your miracles,
You attract many, whom you entice
To read thoroughly the books
Containing those deeds.

May these stupendous deeds not only move
Men to your worship, but also your immense
Gentleness, and indeed your piety toward all,
Anne, those who are stumbling.

You never abandon the miserable when called,
But stand ready for all in dangers.
You hear the suppliants, if they weary
You with reverent prayer.

Whatever will harm us in the highest degree,
Let us refer it all to pious Anne.
She will mitigate our cares, and for us
She will diminish our pains.

The moderator of the starry orb himself
Is her grandson; whatever she asks, she will obtain.
She is the parent of Christ, her own offspring;
What would he deny to Anne?

Anne, hail, venerable mother.
You are the parent of Christ, equally blessed.
Hail, blessed grandson, be with us
Always.

Anne, grant that we may live always
Chaste, serious, and modest, stable in Christ.
Here, may we never, when called upon,
Be deprived of your help.

Hence, may famine, plague, and <term>Enyo</term> <gloss>goddess of war</gloss> be far away.

### Scena Tertia.

Achab maximâ sui populi confusione turbatus per omnes Regiones inquiri jubet Eliam, ut illum (quem admodum putat Sanctus Augustinus) interficiat.

### Scena Quarta.

Exsiccato torrente Carith jubetur Elias ire in Sareptham Sidoniorum; ibi à muliere vidua pascendus, quam invenit colligentem ligna cum filio. Rogat alimentum Elias, cum promissione non defecturæ farinæ, ex qua mulier illi panem subcinericium confecit.

### Scena Quinta.

Vidua Sarepthana hilaris offert Eliæ subcinericium panem. Narrat de farina nihil diminuta, DEO Eliæ benedicit, & rogat Prophetam, vt domi suæ dignetur hospitari.

### Scena Sexta.

Ægrotat filius Viduæ, ac deinde moritur, quem Elias ad vitam revocatum Matri restituit.

### Chorus.

# ACT I.

## PROLOGUE.

Moses, summoned by God's command through an Angel from Limbo <note>the place reserved for the souls of the righteous before Christ</note> to the earth, denounces the crimes of King Ahab and the people of Israel. He rouses the prophet Elijah to rebuke these sins and warns him of the future persecution of the prophets.

->*Scene One.*<-

The prophets of the idol Baal conspire to kill the prophets of the true God. They approach Queen Jezebel, who is cheerfully indulging her senses, and through her, they obtain from King Ahab a decree of death against the true prophets.

->*Scene Two.*<-

Obadiah, the steward of the Royal House and, as some maintain, a secret disciple of Elijah, is aware of the death sentence passed upon the prophets. He diligently searches for those he can save and warns them of the danger and the need for flight. At the risk of his own life, he hides one hundred of them in two caves and provides them with food.

->*Scene Three.*<-

The true prophets of God are sought for execution. Some are captured. Others flee. Some remain in hiding. There are those who, through the force of threats or the hope of reward, are betrayed by informants while in hiding.

<summary>This page introduces the prologue and first three scenes of the first act, detailing the conspiracy of Baal's prophets against the servants of God, Obadiah's attempts to protect them, and the resulting persecution.</summary>

### *Scena Secunda.*

Elias monitus ab Angelo ut Regem adeat, occurrit Abdiae, jubetque renunciari Regi se adesse. Rex irâ commotus Eliam alloquitur.. Elias zelo DEI plenus Regem impietatis & Idololatriae arguit: petitque congregari Prophetas Baalis ut coram populo Israelis coelesti prodigio decernatur an Baal, an DEUS Eliae sit verus DEUS?

### *Scena Tertia.*

Congregatis Baalis Prophetis conuenitur inter illos, & Eliam, futurum illum verum DEUM, ad cujus invocationem bos in holocaustum concisus & super ligna positus nullo igne subjecto, sed cælitùs immisso comburetur. Baalis Prophetae primi suum DEUM à mane ad meridiem frustra inclamant. Tum Elias bovem alterum parat in holocaustum & ligna, quibus comburi debet, ter aquâ mandata aspergi, DEOque invocato statim ignis adest è Coelo & vorat holocaustum.

### *Chorus.*

Intelligentiae Coelos moventes, depulsis signis Coelorum igneis reducunt signa aquatica, & ad pluviam Coelum disponunt.

### *Scena Quarta.*

Post diuturnam trium annorum & amplius siccitatem tandem populus cum gaudio, & ferae cum tripudijs pluviam excipiunt.

### *Scena Quinta.*

Conscius minarum Iezabelis ob interfectos Baalis Prophetas Elias, dimisso puero fugit, cumque mærens & lassus obdormivisset sub Iunipero excitatur ab Angelo, & ab eodem allato cibo refectus jubetur in montem Oreb se recipere.
